#3245. Cannes Protests “Judicial Persecution” Of Iranian Director Jafar Panahi

The Cannes Film Festival has issued a statement protesting recent legal sanctions against Iranian Palme d’Or-winning director Jafar Panahi, including a five-year, one-month prison sentence and travel ban.

The statement comes just three weeks after news broke that Panahi is caught once again in the crosshairs of the Iranian authorities.

“The Festival de Cannes strongly condemns the judicial persecution of Jafar Panahi and calls for the lifting of all restrictions that prevent him from traveling, creating, and expressing himself freely,” said the festival. Related Stories News Cannes Marché & TIFFCOM Commit To Holding Second Edition Of Japan IP Market In 2027 News Jafar Panahi Back In Crosshairs Of Iranian Authorities With Five-Year Sentence

“Like artists, festivals, and cultural institutions around the world, the Festival de Cannes calls on the international community to take action and speak with one voice to prevent his imprisonment. His freedom is not just about one filmmaker, it is about the rights of all artists to think, create, and express themselves without fear of imprisonment,” it continued. Watch on Deadline

“Everyone knows this, and everyone stands up for it: ‘No artist should be imprisoned for their work, their ideas or their expression, in Iran or anywhere.’

Local media reported in mid-October that Panahi, who spent much of 2025 and early 2026 outside of Iran on the awards trail with Cannes Palme d’Or winner It Was Just Sent An Accident, has been given a five-year, one-month prison sentence.

His lawyer Mostafa Nili told local media that Branch 26 of the Tehran Revolutionary Court had slapped Panahi with a five-year sentence, two-year social media and travel ban, and also issued an order for the confiscation of Panahi’s possessions and assets.

Nili and his client paid a visit to the Sentence Enforcement Unit of the Culture and Media Prosecutor’s Office, where they learned that Panahi had been convicted “in absentia” in a separate case.

The director currently has three open cases in Iran but according to Nili had not been officially summoned for hearings, even though he is in the country.

Panahi returned home immediately after the March 15 ceremony for the 2026 Academy Awards in which It Was Just An Accident was nominated and has not left since.

The new sentence comes on top of a separate one-year prison sentence and a two-year travel meted out by the Iranian Branch 26 court in 2025, on charges of “propaganda activities against the system.”

Panahi has long been in the crosshairs of Iran’s hardline Islamic Republic authorities. He spent seven months in the country’s notoriously tough Evin jail after being arrested in July 2022. Iranian authorities reactivated a six-year sentence originally given to Panahi in 2010 alongside a 20-year filmmaking and travel ban.

He had originally gone to the prison to enquire about the whereabouts of fellow filmmakers Mohammad Rasoulof and Mostafa Al-Ahmad who had been arrested a few days previously for criticizing the actions of the authorities in an open letter.

The reactivated sentence was connected to Panahi’s attendance of a funeral in 2009 of a student shot dead in the Green Revolution and his later attempt to shoot a feature set against the backdrop of the uprising. He was released in February 2023 after going on hunger strike.

It seemed for a time that the authorities were softening their stance towards the director after he was granted permission to travel to Cannes for the first time in 15 years in 2025 for the premiere of clandestinely shot film It Was Just An Accident. It went on to win the Palme d’Or and then be Oscar nominated in the Best International Feature Film Category as the French entry.

While on the final stages of awards campaign trail, Panahi publicly denounced a deadly crackdown on pro-democracy protests which swept Iran in January 2026 in which tens of thousands are believe to have died.

In spite of the tense political situation in Iran and potential threat to his own freedom, Panahi vowed to return home as soon as his Oscar contender duties were done and dusted, which he did.

The director has a long relationship with the Cannes Film Festival ever since his first film The White Balloon won the Caméra d’Or in 1995.

A number of his films have played in the festival including Panahi’s films on numerous occasions, including Crimson G ol d , which won the Un Certain Regard Jury Prize in 2003, and 3 F aces, which was presented in Competition in 2018 and won the Best Screenplay Award.

In 2010, he was invited to serve on the jurywhile he was imprisoned in Iran. His seat remained empty during the opening ceremony.

“Fifteen years later, in 2025, Jafar Panahi took the stage to receive the Palme d’Or for I t W a s J ust an A cci d ent. This award honored a career dedicated to defending creative freedom and freedom of expression,” wrote the festival.

#3244. Apple reveals how iCloud+ increases Siri AI and Apple Intelligence usage limits

iOS 27.3 beta 2 is now available, and Apple is adding the ability for users to unlock higher usage limits for Apple Intelligence and Siri AI via iCloud+. Here’s everything you need to know.

From the start, Apple has said that some Siri AI and Apple Intelligence features have usage limits because “they rely on powerful server models.” The company previously outlined that increased access would be available across most iCloud+ subscription plans, and now we have the full details on how this will work.

Apple says the new system applies to several categories of Apple Intelligence features, including:

The usage limits are per device, not per account. This means your iPhone, iPad, and Mac each have separate allowances. Apple isn’t disclosing specific limit numbers. Instead, it says that limits can vary based on the feature, request complexity, system demand, and more.

As you near your limit, you’ll see an alert within whichever feature you’re using. For example, if you are using Image Playground, a message will appear telling you that you’ve almost hit your usage limit for the day. Once you hit the limit, you’ll be prompted to wait for it to reset or upgrade your iCloud+ plan.

If you hit your limit, basic Siri requests will still work. This includes things like setting timers and alarms. Requests that require Siri to understand personal context and perform more complex, multi-step actions, however, are subject to the limits.

For example, asking Siri to find the details of an upcoming dinner reservation in your email and add them to your calendar would count toward your daily limit.

Additionally, each device uses its own standard daily usage limit first. After that, it can tap into the additional capacity included with an eligible iCloud+ subscription:

The usage unlocked by iCloud+ is shared across all devices signed in to your Apple Account, as well as family members sharing your iCloud+ plan. The shared usage is available on a first-come, first-served basis

All limits will reset daily at the same time, and limits don’t roll over. In most cases, limits reset around midnight in your current time zone.

Apple has published a support document with more details.

#3243. When Electric Cars Were for Women

Early carmakers decided women wanted cars that were quiet, clean, and easy to start

Allison Marsh is a professor at the University of South Carolina and the codirector of the Ann Johnson Institute for Science, Technology & Society.

When automobiles were still a novelty, electric cars vied with those powered by steam and internal combustion.

At the turn of the last century, the automobile industry was still new and evolving rapidly. In 1898, there were about 50 carmakers in the United States. A decade later, that number had increased fivefold. In 1901, the companies produced 7,000 vehicles. By 1910, production had reached 181,000.

For several decades, electric cars vied with those powered by steam and internal combustion, and nobody was sure which technology would come out on top. Steam had the legacy of locomotive technology behind it but came with a risk of fire. Steam-powered vehicles could also become exceedingly hot, depending on the placement of the boiler and the steam piping. Both gasoline and electric cars faced logistical challenges: How far could you travel without refueling or charging? You could always throw an extra can of gasoline in the back of the car, but charging a battery involved more planning. The infrastructure for long-distance travel was not yet in place.

Before the invention of the electric starter in 1911, gasoline-powered engines had to be started with a hand crank; once running, they were loud and emitted noxious fumes. Fully electric vehicles, by contrast, were easy to start; you just turned on the main battery switch, often with a key, and there was no foul exhaust to deal with.

Electric carmakers looking for a way to differentiate their products decided that these attributes made their vehicles perfect for women. (Electric cars were also marketed to doctors so that they could make house calls in the middle of the night without waking the neighbors.) General Electric, which made car chargers based on mercury-arc rectifiers, was so captivated by the idea of women driving electric cars that the company created a series of advertisements featuring stylishly dressed women plugging in their cars and posing with their charging stations.

In ads for its electric car chargers, General Electric featured women using the equipment.miSci—Museum of Innovation and Science

A young woman named Fannie Goodnow was an early EV adopter. She owned a 1908 Bailey Victoria Phaeton, an open two-seater that really did look like a horseless carriage, and she used a GE mercury-arc rectifier to charge it.

Electrical engineer Peter Cooper Hewitt invented the mercury vapor lamp, which became the basis for the mercury-arc rectifier used in car-charging systems. Bettmann/Getty Images

Electrical engineer Peter Cooper Hewitt is generally credited with the invention of the mercury-arc rectifier. During the first decade of the 20th century, Hewitt received several U.S. patents for electric lamps and other apparatus for transmitting and using electric currents. U.S. patents 968,896 and 1,163,706, granted to Percy H. Thomas, advanced Hewitt’s designs. Thomas was chief electrician for the Cooper Hewitt Electric Co., which Hewitt had cofounded with George Westinghouse to manufacture and sell his lamps.

The mercury-arc rectifier functioned as a diode. In a car charger like the one Fannie Goodnow used, it converted alternating current from the power grid into direct current needed to charge the car’s battery. A small amount of liquid mercury contained in a glass tube would vaporize and glow as electricity passed through it. Coupled with the carbon anodes, the vapor allowed current to flow in only one direction. This unit took about 12 hours to charge a drained battery.

I couldn’t find any records as to why Fannie Goodnow opted for an electric car. But as a well-to-do woman living in the Boston area, she had more than a half dozen automobile producers to choose from. The one she chose was S.R. Bailey & Co. of Amesbury, Mass.

This early electric car charger used a mercury-arc rectifier to convert AC to DC.Heritage Museums & Gardens

According to Galen Handy, who maintains the Early Electric Vehicles website, Samuel Robinson Bailey started in the carriage and sleigh business as a teenager, winning a best-in-show prize at a carriage exhibition in Portland, Maine, in 1855. Bailey developed a reputation as an inventor and designed processes to streamline the manufacture of his vehicles. He went into business for himself in 1882. Just over a decade later, one of Bailey’s carriages won a gold medal at the 1893 World’s Columbian Exposition in Chicago.

Bailey’s son Edwin attended the exposition, where he likely would have seen a vision of the future: the Morrison electric wagon. This six-passenger, battery-powered vehicle ferried visitors and VIPs around the fairgrounds. It wasn’t long before automobiles began eating into the carriage business. In December 1906, with the carriage industry collapsing, S.R. Bailey & Co. announced it was getting into electric vehicles.

Bailey’s first model, the Victoria Phaeton, used an Edison alkaline battery. Thomas Edison had been working on a lighter, more reliable, and more powerful battery for the auto industry since the 1890s, and announced the achievement with great fanfare in 1903. Unfortunately for Bailey and other carmakers who deployed it, the battery leaked and wouldn’t hold a charge. Edison was forced to go back to the drawing board. By 1910, he had a better battery in production, but by then his friend Henry Ford had introduced the Model T, setting the stage for the internal combustion engine to take over the market.

While Edison toiled to improve his tech, Bailey pivoted to a battery from the Gould Storage Battery Co. of Depew, N.Y. Gould also supplied batteries for railroads, utilities, subways, elevators, and farms. Goodnow’s Victoria Phaeton used a 30-cell lead-acid battery housed in a wooden box that was suspended under the chassis. The standard battery had a range of 64 to 80 kilometers; a larger battery with 50 percent more capacity was available for an upcharge. With the standard battery, the Victoria Phaeton cost US $2,000 (about $73,000 today, or about the list price of an upscale EV like the Audi Q8 or BMW i5).

Fannie Goodnow’s electric car charger now resides at the Heritage Museums & Gardens in Sandwich, Mass. But her 1908 Bailey Victoria Phaeton has been lost to history. Shown here is a 1911 version of that model.Sarah Thornington/Heritage Museums & Gardens

Goodnow installed a mercury-arc rectifier charging station in the barn adjacent to her parents’ summer home in Hull, Mass. Bill Lillie of Vintage Electric Cars notes that the charging plug was of an unusual design. This is, of course, one of the banes of any early adopter: nonstandardized plugs and cables. The Electric Vehicle Association of America, which formed in 1910, tried to put forward a standard so that electric vehicles could be charged at any charging station. (Modern EV owners can no doubt relate.) But savvy electric car owners knew to carry spare plug adapters and cables when traveling.

When Edison’s improved battery was finally available, Bailey began using it in the Victoria Phaeton and then went on a publicity blitz. In September 1910, the carmaker sponsored a round-trip tour from New York to Boston, with a side trip up New Hampshire’s Mount Washington, totaling about 1,600 km. Sadly, the “This Car Climbed Mt. Washington” bumper sticker hadn’t yet become popular.

Thomas Edison supplied the batteries for an electric car made by S.R. Bailey & Co., which then went on a publicity road trip from New York to Boston. miSci—Museum of Innovation and Science

Although Thomas Edison posed for a photo with the new Bailey Victoria Phaeton that featured his new battery, he himself chose a Detroit Electric Victoria for his own use. (Edison was known to be a terrible driver, so someone else likely chauffeured him around.)

Unable to compete against the rising tide of Model Ts, S.R. Bailey sold its factory in 1915, having produced about 500 to 600 electric vehicles.

Although the vehicle Fannie Goodnow chose turned out to be just a blip in automotive history, I like to imagine her driving about town in a beautiful car that embodied all the quirks of early adoption. I hope her friends didn’t make fun of her for investing in electric just before internal combustion took off. I hope she didn’t get stranded without the proper charging cable. I do not know what happened to her or her Victoria Phaeton, but her charging station remained in situ until 2022, when it was donated to the Heritage Museums & Gardens in Sandwich, Mass. Now it stands ready to tell stories of technological change and adoption that continue to resonate today.

Part of a continuing series looking at historical artifacts that embrace the boundless potential of technology.

An abridged version of this article appears in the November 2026 print issue.

She combines her interests in engineering, history, and museum objects to write the Past Forward column, which tells the story of technology through historical artifacts. Marsh is currently working on a book on the history of women in electrical engineering.

Home security cameras have become ordinary household hardware. SafeHome.org’s 2026 survey of 2,435 US adults found that 61% of households have at least one, up from 52% in 2024 and 42% in 2023, while video doorbells have reached 48% of households. Renters drove much of that growth. Their adoption rate jumped from 42% to 54% between 2024 and 2026, which makes sense given how many battery-powered cameras can be mounted without drilling and moved at the end of a lease.

In other words, when looking for one of the best home security cameras, it makes more sense to start with the features and subscription, rather than the headline numbers on the spec sheet. That, of course, can make finding the right one even harder. Here are some things to keep in mind when looking for a home security camera.

Arlo's Essential Wireless Security Camera helps you keep an eye on all the places that matter most. With Smart Detection for people, pets and packages, along with real-time alerts and color night vision, this high-quality security camera will give you peace of mind. Get two wire-free, rechargeable cameras this Black Friday, and with easy installation, they'll be up and running for the holidays.

The best way to figure out what security camera is right for you is to start with thinking about what you actually need a camera for.

A video doorbell suits packages and callers because its head-to-toe view and two-way talk are built around a front door. A driveway or yard needs a weatherproof outdoor camera, while a floodlight camera covers a broader area and adds deterrence. As a rule, cover each entry point instead of asking one camera to watch the entire property.

Prices generally fall into three useful bands. Budget models can be found for as little as $29, but you can still find features like 2K video and a pan-and-tilt designs that physically turn to cover a room. Mid-range models (around $100) offer good value, with additional features or better designs. Premium hardware reaches the $249 level and beyond, where you'll find such things as 4K video.

The number of megapixels figure on the box matters less than how many pixels land on a face. A 4-megapixel camera with a 2,560-pixel-wide image and an 80-degree lens can, under the older IEC 62676-4 identification guideline, identify someone at roughly 20 feet. A 4K camera captures 3,840 pixels across, but pair it with a wider 100-degree lens and that estimate rises only to about 21 feet. The extra pixels have been spent on width, so with the same lens, 4K gives you roughly twice the identification distance of 1080p, not four times.

Get instant access to breaking news, the hottest reviews, great deals and helpful tips.

Treat these numbers as geometry rather than guarantees, especially since the IEC standard for measuring detail at distance was revised in 2025. It uses 500 pixels per meter of scene width for validating a known person and 1,500 for high-certainty identification, while many spec sheets still rely on the older 250-pixel guideline. For a doorbell, 1080p is generally enough because visitors are close. For outdoor cameras, 2K, usually around 2,560 pixels across, is the sensible default. Pay for 4K when you need more detail at distance rather than simply a wider view, and check that your storage and Wi-Fi can handle it.

That said, two ordinary cameras in the right places will often beat one expensive 4K model covering everything badly.

“Spend less time chasing the highest resolution number in isolation. More detail can be useful, but placement, nighttime visibility, and useful notifications deserve just as much attention,” says Lars Felber, director of PR at Eve Systems. “A camera pointed at the wrong part of the porch can miss what matters regardless of its resolution.”

Judge a camera on its night footage, too. Infrared night vision uses light outside the visible spectrum to produce a black-and-white image in darkness, so it can show details relatively cleanly, but not with any color. Color night vision needs ambient light from a streetlamp or porch, or a built-in light — though often color night vision is a little less detailed, and usually can't see as far.

Watch for smeared movement too, since some battery cameras reduce their frame rate at night. Keep the lens away from glass and nearby eaves, which can bounce infrared light back into it.

Power decides where a camera can go and whether it can record continuously. Battery models are the easiest to install and the most renter-friendly, but they sleep until motion wakes them, so you get event clips rather than a full timeline and may lose the moments just before a trigger. Plug-in models remove charging breaks but leave you with a cable to route. Hardwired doorbells and floodlights can support 24/7 recording.

Power over Ethernet, usually shortened to PoE, carries power and data down one network cable for a more dependable connection. PoE requires cabling and a compatible switch or recorder, which is more work than most people want for a single doorbell. Solar models are the compromise. Solar models still have a battery, but solar panels keep the battery topped up so you don't need to worry about manual charging.

A solar panel is often the more practical upgrade for an awkward outdoor mount. Just about every company that makes one of the best outdoor security cameras offers a compatible panel. You’ll need a position with dependable sun, and short winter days can still leave the camera reliant on its battery, though it still beats climbing a ladder every few weeks.

Outdoor hardware also needs a weather rating. IP65, which means dust-tight and protected against low-pressure water jets, is a common floor for outdoor cameras and suits eave-mounted units, while IP66 is the better target for fully exposed walls. Check the stated operating temperature too. Arlo rates the Pro 6 down to −4°F, while cheaper models don’t always cope as well with freezing conditions. If you live somewhere that gets truly cold, like Canada, many models may not work for you.

Before drilling, test Wi-Fi at the exact mount point with your phone. Exterior walls and foil-backed insulation can badly weaken 5GHz Wi-Fi, which is fast but relatively short-ranged. Many budget cameras use only 2.4GHz, which reaches farther but contends with more household congestion.

Finally, check your upload speed if you plan to run several cloud cameras. Local recording to a memory card or hub doesn’t use that upload link, but continuous cloud video can saturate it surprisingly quickly.

Often, the price you pay for the camera itself is just a starting point. You still have to store video — and unless you can do so locally, you may have to pay for a subscription.

A local hub splits the difference. These live in your house, but are connected to your cameras wirelessly, so footage can survive both a damaged camera and an internet outage. A hybrid setup is generally the better choice, with local recording for continuity and cloud copies for important events.

“One of the most important things to look for in a home security camera is if a subscription is required to set up and use the device,” says Carney. “Going into the purchasing process, consumers should be aware that some security companies tack on a required subscription as a hidden cost without being transparent about it at purchase.”

Without a plan, some company's cameras will only let you view live events, and not save recordings, or access all of a camera's features. Be sure to look at the price of the subscription, and see if what's being offered is worth the long-term investment.

Once footage is being recorded, the next problem is getting alerted only when it matters. A camera that pings every time a car passes will eventually be ignored. Custom motion zones, sensible sensitivity controls and reliable person, vehicle and package detection do more for daily use than another AI label. At a door, two-way audio is worth having too, so you can speak to a courier without opening it.

“A camera can be very advanced and still fail at its only job if notifications are delayed,” says Rod Sides, founder of Loxx Boxx. “Worse, if it displays too many notifications in a way that you haven’t customized, you’re more likely to overlook the one important notification that may pop up.”

And don’t forget the microphone, since many cameras record audio by default. Recording a private conversation without everyone’s consent can break the law in all-party consent states such as California. If you don’t need sound or two-way talk, switching it off is the safer default.

“What consumers can spend less time worrying about is having the highest resolution or every bell and whistle on the market,” says Zavin. “Instead, focus on what the camera can actually do when a potential threat arises.”

For most homes, a well-placed 2K camera with accurate detection and a local fallback is the better buy. Step up to 4K or paid AI search if you have a specific use for them, not just because they're available.

Christian de Looper is a freelance writer who has covered every facet of consumer tech, including mobile, audio, home theater, computing, gaming, and even car tech. At Tom’s Guide, Christian covers TV and home theater tech, and has reviewed dozens of TVs, soundbars, and A/V receivers, including those from the likes of Samsung, Hisense, TCL, and Vizio.

#3240. macOS 27.3 includes new privacy controls for Full Disk Access and more

With today’s new macOS 27.3 beta, Apple is implementing several changes as part of this.

In a post on its developer website last month, Apple said some developers are “using Full Disk Access in ways that could put users at risk, exposing everything on their systems.” As such, it said that it would “introduce additional controls to ensure that users who genuinely wish to grant an app this extraordinary level of access can only do so with very explicit user action.”

In macOS 27.2, “Device Control and Data Access” is a unified toggle in System Settings, where Apple says that apps with that level of access can “view and send email, edit contacts and photos, monitor your keyboard, track websites, record your screen, control any app on your Mac, and more.”

In macOS 27.3, Apple is splitting “Device Control and Data Access” into two categories:

For the latter, users will be able to specify which apps an automation tool can access rather than granting it unrestricted control. For instance, you could give an app access to the Mail app, but not Messages.

macOS 27.3 also adds an option for users to require an app to request permission every time it needs access, rather than granting it access indefinitely.

Apple is also introducing a new menu bar indicator that will provide additional transparency when an app is controlling another app with System and App Protection Override. This is designed to let users know when an automation tool is interacting with apps and information in the background.

Crucially, Apple isn’t removing the ability to give an app Full Disk Access. If you deem it necessary, you can still give an app Full Disk Access. However, Apple is redesigning the approval process to make the implications of that decision more obvious.

macOS 27.3 will display a more detailed explanation about the protections being bypassed and the types of personal information that could be exposed.

Users can also choose to grant an app access to specific folders instead of their entire Mac. For example, an app that only needs to work with files in a particular folder won’t get unrestricted access to everything else.

Any app you’ve already given Full Disk Access will still have that access. Previously granted permissions will remain in effect, and those apps will continue functioning as they do today without any approval required.

Apple has published a new support document detailing the Full Disk Access updates.

macOS 27.3 now warns you before giving an app full disk accessThat warning prompt is pretty scary! pic.twitter.com/J2qCKVWJRx

Apple says the underlying APIs aren’t changing, but developers will need to update their apps to account for situations where users grant limited access rather than unrestricted permissions.

Finally, Apple says developers of backup apps and assistive technologies can request entitlements that allow them to maintain the same experience for new installations as before macOS 27.3. Apple has already identified popular apps that rely on these permissions, and those apps will continue working as expected without requiring an entitlement.

Developers can read more on Apple’s Developer website.

I have this running bit where I call Robert Pattinson my girlfriend. It started sometime after "The Lighthouse" because old men gone bitter with yearning is very much my brand of terminally ill brain worm, and the joke's only gotten funnier with the stellar year the "Twilight" star's had. Yesterday, Amazon MGM Studios announced that Pattinson is taking up the mantle of 007, and I broke the news to the group chat with the following message: "my girlfriend is gonna be James Bond!" No explanation needed.

I've never seen a James Bond movie all the way through, a fact that shocked my (mostly male) coworkers this morning. Now that my favorite weird little guy is in the lead, I'm willing to break that streak. Before you go calling me a rabid fangirl, I have another confession: I first watched "Twilight" all the way through this year. I attempted once in high school but had to bail at the baseball scene where the level of unabashed white corniness on display had my eyes nearly rolling out of my skull.

No, my excitement for Pattinson's 007 reign doesn't stem from nostalgia, but from a quiet fascination that's sparked into an obsession over the past decade. This, the man who insists he's "spiritually Gen Z" despite pushing 40, who lies in interviews for fun, who dragged millions of screaming fans into theaters by being a brooding, sexy vampire for a series he openly despises. And I suspect his casting has activated those same millennial women like sleeper agents who will no doubt propel this latest Bond run into one of the most commercially successful to date. With many, like myself, turning out for their first Bond venture in theaters ever.

Action films are a notable blind spot in my cinema knowledge, one that I've been trying to fill in recent years since writing about streaming for Tom's Guide. It's not that I avoided them, per say, just that they didn't immediately appeal to me in the same way as my favorite genres — horror, art house, and damn near anything animated — did.

All the Jason Bournes, John Wicks, and Ethan Hunts of the world struck me as carbon copies of one another made in a lab to be propelled through one bombastic shoot out after the next. Now that I've caught up on a few of these iconic franchises, that opinion still rings true, though I've gained an appreciation for the kind of high-octane set pieces action fans still talk about to this day.

With Pattinson at the helm of the next Bond film, for the first time in my life, I'm excited to see a 007 movie in theaters. His talent and magnetism, even as some of the most pathetic characters I've ever seen on screen, is something straight out of the golden age of Hollywood.

Today's Bond announcement is the cherry on top of a year that's cemented Pattinson as a once in a generation acting talent. Between making our skin crawl as the charismatically slimy Chris Hansen in "Primetime" to going viral for shouting “somebody get these beggars out of here” in Christopher Nolan’s blockbuster megahit “The Odyssey" and proving once again that no one does pathetic quite as well as he does in "The Drama," it's been a banner year for Pattison.

Sign up to the weekly Tom's Streaming Guide to stay in the loop with the latest releases and top recommendations across your favorite streaming services. We’ve got you covered with a complete guide on what’s worth watching.

The British actor most known for his roles as Edward Cullen in “Twilight,” Cedric Diggory in "Harry Potter," and Bruce Wayne in Matt Reeves’ “The Batman” series will now succeed Daniel Craig as everyone's favorite suave superspy. There's no release date yet for Pattinson's debut as 007, though we do know Denis Villeneuve, who has already worked with Pattinson on the upcoming “Dune Part 3,” will be at the helm with a script by "Peaky Blinders" creator Steven Knight.

It's clear Amazon MGM is trying to appeal to younger viewers with this pick too. After being around for over 70 years, James Bond's built a reputation as your father's (or maybe even grandfather's) favorite spy franchise. As Bruce Wayne in "The Batman," Pattinson proved he can bring a fresh edge to an iconic character without losing the mass appeal that makes a franchise work. With "The Batman" sequel currently in production, he’s also firmly established as a leading man audiences will turn out to see. For a franchise looking to usher in its next era, that's a pretty convincing résumé.

By the way if you have seen some Bond movies, why not try playing our multiple choice Bond quiz, below?

#3238. Guarding the Gates of Knowledge

AI can fake a plausible paper at the push of a button. Can detection tools and peer review keep up?

Harry Goldstein is Editor in Chief of IEEE Spectrum.

A recent scroll through social media got me thinking about trust. About half my feed was filled with AI slop that astute users would call out as being machine-generated, often to the embarrassment of the rube who unknowingly spread it and sometimes to the delight of the poster who shared it deliberately because they found it amusing or useful for sowing confusion.

Remember the good old days of GPT-3 when we could ask the chatbot anything and it would almost instantly and very confidently spit back a plausible but false answer? That’s when the word “hallucination” as applied to AI answers entered the lexicon. Six years and several versions of a few different chatbots later, I still can’t trust the answers I get, even though Claude or Gemini often do useful work for me. That’s the thing about current AI: Trust but verify. And verify you must.

Apply that maxim at scale to maintain the integrity of the scientific record and you get an idea of the challenge facing publishers of peer-reviewed scholarship. In “I Used AI to Fake a Scientific Paper,” freelance writer and doctor of applied mathematics Benjamin Skuse tells the story of the human gatekeepers trying to beat back the rising tide of AI slop by attempting to get his own AI-generated papers past IEEE’s defenses.

“He basically hit ‘run experiment’ and ‘write paper.’ And then he didn’t do a damn thing to it.” —Eliza Strickland

As features and AI beat editor Eliza Strickland told me, Skuse was surprised at just how effortless it was to generate a paper that was more or less plausible and more or less science. For one of his experiments, “he basically hit ‘run experiment’ and ‘write paper,’” she said. “And then he didn’t do a damn thing to it. He just launched it into the maw of the publishing engine.”

Skuse discovered that the combination of IEEE’s human-review processes and research-integrity checker programs are currently keeping pace in what amounts to a cat-and-mouse game against people using free tools. But the more advanced LLMs are no longer making the same dumb mistakes the free versions do. That leaves publishers locked in an arms race between increasingly plausible slop and the systems aimed at detecting it.

Scholarly publishers aren’t the only ones trying to hold the line against slop. So is that global depository of human-generated knowledge, Wikipedia. For this month’s Five Questions, Strickland interviewed Ellia Lebleu, a founding member of WikiProject AI Cleanup, a volunteer effort to detect and delete AI-generated material from the platform. Lebleu’s team is confronting the same problem as commercial publishers, but with fewer people and fewer tools.

“Wikipedia is known as a repository of human-generated information, and they want to hold on to that,” says Strickland. “Who knows how long they’ll be able to do that.”

If we can’t collectively assume that the scientific record is trustworthy or that basic facts about the world are accurate, then our understanding of what is real unspools into uncertainty. Perhaps that delights quantum scientists and the grifters who thrive in an information environment where there is no shared reality. But that uncertainty ultimately undermines trust in the institutions that exist to curate the corpus of human knowledge and to promote the advancement of science and technology for the benefit of humanity.

Or maybe in a world where AI is doing the science and writing the papers, it won’t matter whether or not humans trust the outputs. As Strickland put it, “Doesn’t it just feel crazy that we’ll have AI writing for other AIs at some point? We’ll just get left out of the loop.”

Harry Goldstein is Editor in Chief of IEEE Spectrum.

#3237. iOS 27.3 adds new face unlock feature for iPhone Duo

In today’s iOS 27.3 beta release, Apple is introducing two changes for iPhone Duo users. Most notably, it adds a new face recognition option that lets you unlock your iPhone Duo by looking at it.

Apple is also adding an option to have your iPhone Duo lock when you close it.

You can enable the new option to unlock your iPhone Duo with the front camera in Settings, under Touch ID & Passcode, after updating to iOS 27.3. When enabled, your iPhone Duo will unlock after recognizing your face.

Use the front camera, along with a recent Touch ID or passcode authentication, to quickly unlock iPhone Duo when it’s closed. Face recognition data never leaves your device.

This isn’t Face ID. This new option on iPhone Duo uses the front camera on the outer iPhone Duo display to recognize your face. The iPhone Duo doesn’t have the hardware needed for Face ID.

Because this isn’t as secure as Face ID, Touch ID, or your passcode, Apple has implemented a few guardrails. First, the setting only works to unlock your iPhone Duo. To use Apple Pay, access your passwords, unlock apps, and do other things that require authentication, you’ll have to use Touch ID or enter your passcode.

This face recognition feature also has a time-based limitation. After 45 minutes of inactivity, you have to authenticate with Touch ID or your passcode. That is, if you go 45 minutes without unlocking your iPhone Duo, the facial recognition feature is disabled until you enter your passcode or use Touch ID.

Finally, this new feature also doesn’t work when using the iPhone Duo unfolded. When unfolded, you still have to use Touch ID or your passcode to unlock the device.

Second, iOS 27.3 adds an option to lock your iPhone Duo when you close it. You can enable this in Settings, under Display & Brightness. Once enabled, your iPhone Duo will lock when you fold, rather than transition from the inner display to the outer display.

Many iPhone Duo users (myself included) have said Apple should do this. Personally, I’ve been using a shortcut to mimic this behavior, but I’m glad to see that Apple has listened to user feedback and added a default setting for it.

Attendees in Region 4 learn about AI, cybersecurity, and more

Siva Rama Krishna Varma Bayyavarapu is an IEEE senior member and secretary of the IEEE Computer Society’s Central Indiana Chapter.

To help engineers keep up with emerging technologies such as AI, cloud computing, and sustainable infrastructure, and learn how they can be applied in practice, the IEEE Computer Society’s Central Indiana Chapter recently launched its Tech Talk Series.

The live webinar series connects IEEE members, undergrad and graduate students, and engineering professionals from IEEE Region 4 with industry practitioners. The monthly sessions have covered AI governance and security, agentic systems, and related topics. The sessions featured speakers from Apple, software company Tavant, and cybersecurity concern Zscaler.

Upcoming sessions and registration details are available on the IEEE Region 4 virtual events calendar.

Rather than presenting on emerging technologies only at a conceptual level, speakers discussed the design decisions behind specific tools and systems, how the systems are structured, and implementation challenges. They also shared lessons learned from using the tools in their daily work.

Sessions also include technical walkthroughs and practical examples.

The live format allows attendees to discuss and compare their approaches when evaluating and implementing new technologies with those used by other organizations.

The organizers chose to make the series virtual so that chapter members and other attendees could participate in technical discussions with engineers from major technology companies and eliminate the need to travel.

For young professionals, the sessions connect what they’ve learned in a classroom with the realities of the workplace.

Technical programs such as the Tech Talk Series give professionals and students access to expertise, help create connections across career levels, and make important engineering discussions available to a broader community.

Attendees learn how practitioners approach projects such as system architecture, reliability, security, governance, and product delivery. For experienced professionals, the talks offer a forum to examine new ways of designing, securing, and operating software systems, and compare technical approaches. They can ask questions relevant to systems being evaluated or deployed within their organization.

The most recent webinar, Feeding and Fencing AI Agents: Engineering Governed Agentic Systems on Real-Time Data, featured Gajendra Babu Thokala, a senior engineering leader at Apple in Seattle.

The IEEE senior member explained how teams can move beyond adding isolated AI features to applications and instead build governed AI-agent systems that use real-time business data to complete multistep business workflows.

Another recent session, Building AI Native Products: A Playbook for Agentic Systems, explored how products built around AI agents differ from traditional software. It also covered how agentic systems can help users complete multistep tasks and workflows. IEEE Senior Member Sandeep Shivam, a product and technology leader at Tavant in Dallas, led the webinar.

Those two sessions illustrate the series’ purpose: helping participants understand what a technology can do and what is required to use it responsibly.

Future sessions are being planned on areas including enterprise AI, software reliability, and responsible AI usage. In addition to speakers from technology companies, the chapter also plans to invite speakers from startups, universities, and research organizations.

Upcoming sessions are expected to cover cloud platforms, enterprise integrations, and the responsible development of AI systems.

Technical programs such as the Tech Talk Series give professionals and students access to expertise, help create connections across career levels, and make important engineering discussions available to a broader community.

Undergraduate and graduate students are invited to participate to gain exposure to technical decision-making and challenges encountered in professional engineering environments.

A combination of tech and practical steps can keep your property safe

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

As we head into the winter (at least in the Northern hemisphere), it's getting darker, earlier. That means that by the time you get home from work, it might already be dark. Some police departments have noticed the same shift and are already planning around it. For example, as daylight saving time ended, the Palos Verdes Estates Police Department in California warned residents that an early sunset gives burglars more chances to spot homes that look unoccupied, and urged people to leave a few interior lights on or use timers, and to keep entryways lit. It's a useful starting point, and a fairly simple one.

But the risk is actually more complicated than the old image of a burglar creeping around at midnight, and so is the defense. Good locks, lighting and habits do a lot of the work, and many of those checks cost almost nothing. A camera or alarm then adds a layer on top, since it shows you what's happening and lets you act on it.

The darker months have arrived, and Arlo's Essential Outdoor Pan Tilt Zoom Security Camera's 360-degree pan and 180-degree tilt capabilities keep an eye on every corner of your property with an integrated spotlight and color night vision. Automatic motion tracking follows activity so you can stay aware of what's happening, and Smart Detection for people, vehicles, pets and packages helps you distinguish between a cat passing through your backyard and a potential security threat.

Thankfully, burglaries are on the decline. The FBI's 2024 burglary rate of 229.2 per 100,000 people was about 69% below the 2005 rate, and the FBI's 2025 data show burglary falling roughly another 16% in 2025.

But falling crime doesn't make prevention optional, because the FBI's 2024 data show that just 15.9% of property crimes were cleared by arrest or exceptional means, and burglary has run a bit lower, at 14.1% in 2019. Getting property back is, realistically, a much weaker plan than keeping someone out.

Package theft is harder to pin down. In Security.org's 2026 survey, 30% of American adults said they'd had a package stolen at some point, up from 24% a year earlier, though the survey wasn't weighted and the increase alone doesn't prove the rate has risen. It does put the exposed parts of a property, including porches, driveways, yards and garages, at the center of a winter plan, since long nights make an approach much easier.

Winter doesn't turn burglars into night owls, but it does change when your home is most exposed. In the Bureau of Justice Statistics' analysis of household burglary, which covers 2003 to 2007, 43% of burglaries of empty homes happened between 6 a.m. and 6 p.m., compared with 26% overnight. In winter, though, sunset moves into the commute window, so a house that's empty and unlit at 5:30 p.m. can look as unoccupied as one at midnight. And the evening stakes are higher, since someone was home in 61% of nighttime burglaries versus 33% of daytime ones.

A sizable share of break-ins also don't need force. The FBI's 2019 breakdown classed 37.8% of burglaries as unlawful entry with no force used. In the dark, an unlocked back door or ground-floor window is easier to try without anyone noticing, which is why the winter checklist starts with locks.

Get instant access to breaking news, the hottest reviews, great deals and helpful tips.

Lock everything, even when you're home, and that includes first-floor windows and any upstairs window reachable from a flat roof or ladder.

On main doors, a deadbolt offers far more resistance than a simple spring latch. Fit it with long screws that anchor the strike plate, the metal plate around the lock bolt, into the frame rather than just the decorative trim. Look for a deadbolt certified to the ANSI/BHMA A156.40 residential standard, ideally with an A grade for security. One of the best smart locks can help too — most offer an auto-lock setting (make sure it's switched on), so even if you forget to lock the door, it won't remain unlocked.

Windows need more than a handle pulled shut. Fit a working lock to every accessible window, and add stops that limit how far it can open. A wooden or metal bar in a patio door's track stops it from sliding, even when the latch is easily broken.

A peephole or door chain gives you a way to check a caller before opening up. Check ID from anyone claiming to be from a utility company, and be especially skeptical of urgent repair offers after bad weather. The FTC warns that scammers often turn up after severe weather, pushing homeowners to sign a contract right away or pay up front, and advises confirming a contractor's license and insurance before agreeing to anything.

Outside, lock the side gate, shed and garage, since long winter nights make outbuildings an easier target. Put ladders and tools away, since they can also help someone reach or force the house. Frost or obscure garage windows too, so nobody can casually browse your belongings from the street.

The boundary of the property matters too. Low front hedges preserve visibility, while gravel makes a quiet approach considerably harder. Anti-climb paint can make fences difficult to grip and marks anyone who touches it, but pair it with warning signs and follow the product's reapplication instructions closely.

Finally, photograph valuables and record serial numbers in an inventory stored somewhere secure. An ultraviolet pen can add ownership details that aren't normally visible, while a forensic marking kit links items to a unique registered code. Neither will stop a theft, but both can help police identify recovered property and make an insurance claim less painful.

One way to help prevent break-ins is to make your home look occupied even when it's not. Start outside with motion-activated lights at entrances, along driveways and on paths. For a side passage or secluded corner, a dusk-to-dawn light switches on automatically when daylight fades, while a solar model avoids running a cable. Smart bulbs and floodlights can go a step further, with schedules tied to local sunset so they shift automatically as the days get shorter, or by switching on when a camera or sensor detects motion.

Aim the light at the approach rather than into a camera lens or a neighbor's window. The goal is to expose movement and give any camera a usable image, not to turn the whole yard into a stadium.

Inside, put a few lamps on timers or smart plugs that switch on around dusk, and vary the schedule if you're away. A smart plug also lets you adjust the lights from your phone if you're delayed getting home or traveling, so the house doesn't sit dark on the one night it matters. Leaving one light on all day can have the opposite effect, because a lamp burning at midday suggests that nobody is there to turn it off.

It's also worth closing curtains or blinds in the evening so screens and valuables aren't visible, and asking a neighbor to collect mail and deliveries.

Then there's the use of other smart security devices. The best home security cameras, of course, are a major one. Place cameras around the routes someone would actually use. The front step matters, but so do the side gate and rear entrance. Good lighting on those approaches will usually do more for night footage than a bigger night-vision range claim, because you need enough detail to identify a face at the gate rather than simply spot a shape. Many smart cameras also let you draw activity zones, so you're alerted to someone at the gate but not to every passing car or neighbor, and models with a built-in spotlight or two-way audio let you light up the area or speak to a visitor from your phone.

The evidence broadly supports that layered approach. A 2019 systematic review of 40 years of research, led by Eric Piza, found that closed-circuit television systems were associated with a significant and modest decrease in crime, with better results when cameras were combined with other measures, so a camera on its own isn't really a perimeter.

Visible alarms still have real value, and in a UNC Charlotte study of 422 convicted burglars, 60% said an alarm would make them choose another target. Monitoring is the part that turns a notification into action. A monitored service watches alerts constantly and can escalate them when you don't respond.

It's also worth making sure your cameras are charged up properly. The usual advice for battery cameras is to keep a second charged pack to swap in, or add a compatible solar panel or USB-C charger where conditions allow. A solar panel won't perform miracles on a shaded wall in December, of course, so keep in mind where the sun will hit when it is out.

Apart from standard cameras, a smart video doorbell can help too. The front door, of course, is where deliveries and visitors arrive. With a smart doorbell, you can see and talk to them straight from your phone, even when you're not there.

The cheapest useful check is to simply walk around your property at dusk and look at it as a stranger would. Can someone reach the back gate unseen? Are ladders out, valuables visible through a window, or packages sitting on the step?

Start with those basics. Good locks, sensible lighting and a routine for looking occupied come first. Then add monitoring that fits your home, whether that's a visible alarm or a well-placed camera, and extend the same attention to sheds, cars and parcels.

Before you travel, test the alarm sensors, clean the cameras, charge or replace batteries in cameras and smart locks, confirm that auto-lock and your lighting schedules are working, confirm that alerts reach someone who can act on them, and check the policy's unoccupied limit.

You don't need to overhaul everything at once to improve the odds. A locked door, a lit approach and a delivery that isn't sitting outside for six hours go a long way, and a camera or alarm that alerts you when something does happen makes those habits more effective.

#3231. Why a Mathematician Is Chasing Eclipses With Algorithms and Cameras

With custom-built gear, his team seeks to solve a long-standing solar mystery

Advanced image-processing software developed by Miloslav Druckmüller combines scores of individual images, captured during a total solar eclipse and painstakingly calibrated. The techniques reveal fine details in the sun’s corona, which is white in this image. The tiny pink shapes seen along portions of the edge of the blacked-out solar disk are prominences, which are extensions of relatively cool plasma that can jut out hundreds of thousands of kilometers into space.

The sun hangs low over the plains of Castile and León, in the north-central region of Spain. But from a slope of the mountain Pico Trigaza, it appears that a few puffy white clouds have started to block the sun. That’s vexing.

A group of researchers, some wearing cardboard eclipse glasses, is clustered around sets of portable telescopes and cameras connected to laptops. All this gear is scattered on tabletops perched on the mountainside. On the computer screens, the sun’s disk looks like a deep orange crescent that is slowly waning. That’s because the moon began to crawl across it about half an hour ago. In 25 minutes, it will obscure the sun completely, producing an eerie and wondrous phenomenon—a total solar eclipse.

In the late-summer, late-afternoon heat, the researchers watch anxiously as those fluffy clouds linger around the sun. From an abandoned hut on the slope a few meters above, where the researchers have set up camp, one of the grad students emerges and nods toward the cloud formation. “Do you think it will dissolve?” he blurts out.

“It will.” Miloslav Druckmüller glances calmly at his group of doctoral candidates, now making final checks of the equipment in preparation for totality. Here in Spain, on this 12th day of August, Druckmüller is getting ready for his 19th solar eclipse. He knows from long experience that weather can turn quickly when the moon’s shadow suddenly pushes the temperature down. Plus, there’s no sense in riling up the grad students any more than they already are.

Miloslav Druckmüller led the design and construction of a unique optical instrument that incorporates eight astrocameras. Each is equipped with a spectral filter for sensing and recording specific emission spectra from the solar corona. Each of those spectra, in turn, is associated with a particular ionic species of iron atoms. Because the temperature needed to ionize iron varies depending on the ionic species, analyzing the locations and relative abundance of these ionic species offers valuable insights into the distribution of heat in the corona.Václav Široký

During totality, the moon blocks the overwhelming glare of the solar disk, revealing delicate structures in the sun’s outer atmosphere, the corona. Using custom-built telescope systems and image-processing techniques that Druckmüller has spent decades developing, the researchers aim to gain insights into the processes in this enigmatic region that is otherwise hard to study. In addition to imaging the visible coronal light, the team will try to track the dispersal of superhot ions of iron into interplanetary space, which could give rare insights into the pattern of heat emanating from the corona.

And they’ll have 107 seconds to do all that.

Druckmüller is a professor of mathematics and image processing at the Brno University of Technology in the Czech Republic and a leading figure in the Solar Wind Sherpas, an international team that studies the sun’s corona during total eclipses. In the solar eclipse world, he is nothing short of a legend, albeit a reluctant one.

An image from Miloslav Druckmüller’s first solar-eclipse expedition, to Hungary, vividly shows Baily’s Beads. These elongated white lights along a piece of the left edge of the blacked-out solar disk are caused by beams of sunlight shining through gaps in the irregular lunar surface during the eclipse. The pink shapes are solar prominences, which are jets of plasma extending out into space and held in place by the sun’s intense magnetic field.

He photographed his first solar eclipse in 1999, in what he thought would be a one-off lark. During that eclipse, the moon’s deep shadow missed Druckmüller’s native Czechia by just a few tens of kilometers, so he chased it to Hungary with a 30-year-old Soviet MTO 1,000-millimeter lens. All he remembers from that day is the rush of adrenaline he felt while trying to find the sun in the sky with the lens’s minuscule field of view and keep it in focus for the two minutes of the eclipse.

He insists that he has never enjoyed any of the eclipses he has photographed. “In fact, I have never properly seen any of those eclipses. You are just watching the screens, making sure that it’s all doing what it’s supposed to do. There are so many things that can go wrong and you can’t redo it.”

A composite sequence of photographs shows the 12 August 2026 solar eclipse as seen from a slope of the mountain Pico Trigaza in Spain.

Despite Druckmüller’s outward tranquility on this Spanish hillside, the stakes are high. Just 45 minutes ago, his group heard from their colleagues in Iceland, where viewing conditions had promised to be better than in Spain. But a vast low-pressure system had clouded the entire sky, leaving all three Iceland teams without a view.

On the Pico Trigaza mountain in Spain, two postgraduate researchers used a laser to get a rough, initial alignment for the tracking mount of an optical instrument. The alignment was necessary to precisely compensate for the Earth’s motion.

The corona has been a mystery for centuries. Though dimmer—by a factor of a million—than the sun’s visible surface, the corona is nevertheless extremely hot: about a million degrees Celsius compared to 5,500 degrees on the surface. Because the sun’s nuclear fusion engine churns at the star’s heart, it might seem that temperatures should fall farther from the core.

To observe the faint corona in visible light, researchers must block the sun’s ferocious glare. Specialized telescopes called coronagraphs do this with an opaque disk called an occulter. But because light bends around the occulter’s edges in an effect called diffraction, it must block an area much larger than that of the solar disk to prevent light from spilling over and ruining the images. But doing so means obstructing the inner part of the corona, which harbors the most important processes that underpin the puzzling phenomena of the sun’s upper atmosphere.

That’s why total eclipses matter so much to solar physicists. By sheer chance, the moon is exactly the right size and at just the right distance to completely cover the sun during a total solar eclipse. Because the moon is so far away from Earth, the view is not marred by diffraction, and the corona reveals itself nearly all the way down to the sun’s surface.

As astrocameras recorded spectral data about the sun’s corona, a laptop computer [on table, at left] displayed the phase of the eclipse.

Space probes can image the solar surface in other wavelengths, but those views have limitations, too. Spacecraft such as NASA’s Solar Dynamics Observatory do see the innermost parts of the corona in extreme ultraviolet light, explains Shadia Habbal, a solar physicist at the University of Hawaii and leader of the Solar Wind Sherpas project. “But it cuts off very quickly, so you don’t see its extension into space as well as we can see it in the visible emission lines” during an eclipse. “That’s the biggest advantage,” she says, of solar eclipse photography.

The European Proba-3 mission, launched in 2024, simulates total solar eclipses by flying two spacecraft in a formation 150 meters apart with one acting as an occulter and the other as the telescope. The instruments aboard that satellite, however, have limitations compared to the equipment used by the Solar Wind Sherpas team.

When Druckmüller developed the film from his 1999 eclipse expedition, the photographs didn’t do justice to the event’s eerie beauty. He spent countless evenings applying his expertise in numerical image processing in an attempt to re-create in his photographs the sights he witnessed in that Hungarian corn field.

It took two years, but eventually he succeeded. Where before there were dull views of the blackened lunar disk surrounded by the blunt wisps of the corona, Druckmüller revealed the subtlest details of the magnetic field lines stretching from the sun far into space. As his photographs circulated among solar physicists, invitations to eclipse expeditions began to arrive.

Solar researchers Miloslav Druckmüller and Shadia Habbal have been collaborating for two decades and 15 eclipses.

Habbal learned about the images from a Ph.D. student who had seen them at a conference presentation that didn’t credit Druckmüller. When Habbal’s team later published the images in a paper, they misattributed them to another researcher. Druckmüller found out through an astrophysicist friend. “I wrote her a rather disappointed email and she responded within 10 minutes,” Druckmüller recalls. “She really didn’t have a clue.”

The error was corrected, and within weeks, Habbal and Druckmüller began a collaboration that grew into a friendship. “Milos’s processing brings out details that nobody has seen before, and they tell you a lot about very tiny features in the corona that you don’t see otherwise,” says Habbal.

Capturing the corona’s delicate structures means finding a way to show its brightest and faintest features in the same image. “During the solar eclipse, the contrast between the darkest and brightest parts of the corona is enormous, possibly one to a million,” Druckmüller explains. “But a computer monitor only allows you to display a contrast ratio of one to about 800.” (Some modern monitors, particularly OLED ones, can deliver higher contrast ratios.)

The human eye can adjust to this enormous range of brightness, allowing an observer to see both the bright corona and the faint stars and planets that briefly emerge in the darkened sky. To bring those details together in a photograph, Druckmüller uses custom image-processing algorithms to combine exposures that capture different parts of that range.

Researchers Martin Šebek and Peter Urgoš make fine adjustments to the focus and alignment of the astrocameras on a key optical instrument before the 12 August solar eclipse.

To create a single image, Druckmüller’s teams need to take 200 individual frames during the eclipse at exposure times ranging from 0.001 second to two seconds. The data must then be calibrated against a vast number of reference images to filter out noise and imperfections. Flat fields, which depict a uniform light background, help correct for defects caused by telescope optics, dust spots, and variations in pixel sensitivity. Dark frames, taken with light blocked from the sensor, help correct for artifacts created by the camera’s image sensor itself. “It takes the computer more than two days to process one image,” Druckmüller says. Including the calibration data, a single finished image requires about 3,000 input frames.

Since 2008, teams directed by Habbal and Druckmüller have traveled to every total solar eclipse, spreading out across multiple locations to hedge against bad weather. About half of the teams return with usable data. For the others, it’s just a short and stressful voyage. For the 12 August eclipse, three groups deployed to Iceland and two to Spain.

The teams seek sites close to the center of the band of totality, where the moon blocks the sun for longest. In Spain, the 12 August band of totality cut across the north of the country; the center line of the shadow passed within 11 kilometers of Pico Trigaza, promising Druckmüller and his colleagues a precious 107 seconds of totality.

But duration is only part of the calculation. Totality on Pico Trigaza will commence 51 minutes before sunset, with the sun just 8 degrees above the horizon. That low, the rays must pass through a much thicker layer of the atmosphere than when the sun is higher in the sky, increasing the light distortion that complicates photography. At the researchers’ camp on Pico Trigaza, 1,600 meters above sea level, the thinner air should help a bit.

An abandoned hut on the mountain Pico Trigaza in Spain was spruced up so that it could serve as a home base for the research team recording the 12 August solar eclipse.

“Iceland would have been a much better place for us than Spain because the sun was higher up, some 25 degrees above the horizon,” Druckmüller says wistfully. But Iceland’s notoriously unpredictable weather made Spain an essential backup.

If you pack a van with thousands of dollars’ worth of cameras and optical gear and then set out on a 2,351-kilometer journey, you shouldn’t be surprised if you finish the trip with a few striking photographs [top]. The sleeping arrangements for the grad students at the Pico Trigaza hut [bottom] were spartan, but the views were first-rate.Top: Martin Šebek; Bottom: Václav Široký

On the mountain, locals have spruced up a rustic, long-unused hut for the researchers, running power cables from a nearby telecommunication outpost and bringing in a water tank. Five Ph.D. students drove more than 2,000 kilometers from Brno and have spent nearly a week preparing the equipment. Druckmüller and his wife joined them two days before the eclipse. They cook on a small propane grill and sleep in sleeping bags on yoga mats. “We have plenty of space here to set up our telescopes, beautiful views, and a roof over our heads,” Druckmüller says with a grin. “It’s perfect.”

But even the best equipment and a carefully chosen site count for nothing if the clouds roll in. “So much work goes into the preparations and then, if you end up with nothing, you just feel terrible sadness,” says Jana Hoderová, an assistant professor of mathematics at Brno University of Technology and one of Druckmüller’s key collaborators.

As the moon continues to slide in front of the solar disk, the pesky cumulus cloud that kept everybody on edge begins to dissolve. It’s 10 minutes to totality. The relief is palpable.

The countdown on the computers that control the cameras has begun. The screens are now showing only a tiny orange sliver, and the evening is becoming perceptibly less bright.

Twenty astrophotography cameras, most of them drawing power from a car battery that was also buffering the cameras from any grid instabilities, are pointed at the sun. Alongside equipment capturing the corona’s visible light, the team has built an assembly of eight cameras to detect light emitted by various iron ions that arise in the corona.

Among the optical gear assembled at Pico Trigaza to capture the 12 August solar eclipse was a unique instrument designed to record the distributions of iron ions in the corona [at left]. Václav Široký

Those instruments looking for iron ions have been put together with resourcefulness and thrift. A colleague of Druckmüller’s laser-cut the aluminum plates holding the carefully aligned lenses in exchange “for two bottles of whisky.” The brackets and attachments were 3D-printed at Brno University of Technology. The lenses, produced for the defunct camera maker Contax, were bought at steep discounts on eBay. By far the most expensive elements are interference filters that isolate the wavelengths emitted by the iron ions.

Around the blackened solar disk rises the magnificent golden halo of the corona. In the hush on the mountainside, it seems that even the birds have gone still.

“That’s something nobody else in the world can do,” Druckmüller says with visible satisfaction. The unique technology, codeveloped with Habbal’s Hawaii team, has already enabled researchers to map the distribution of temperatures across the entire corona and to discover previously unseen structures, dubbed “smoke rings,” in the coronal plasma. The photographs also revealed the boundary region where the solar plasma becomes so thin that its ions stop colliding.

The optical assembly designed to record the distributions of iron ions in the corona is outfitted with astrocameras, each of which captures spectra from a different ionic species. To do that, each astrocamera is equipped with a spectral filter whose bandwidth is so narrow—one nanometer—that the filter appears as a mirror.Martin Fornůsek

“Iron is the most abundant of the heavy elements that we see in the solar corona,” says Habbal. “And because the corona is so hot, the iron atoms lose electrons and get ionized. The larger the loss, the higher the temperature.”

For example, a temperature of around 1.6 million °C is necessary to produce an iron ion that has lost 12 electrons. But only 1.4 million °C is needed to strip an iron atom of 11 electrons. Once it’s in a particular electrical state, the ion retains its specific ionization, even as it travels outward with the solar wind. Each of those ions, whether +11 or +12, emits a different wavelength of light, allowing the researchers to map not just temperatures within the corona, but also how those iron ions spread into interplanetary space and distribute heat. Habbal and her colleagues had long been trying to image those iron ions during solar eclipses. But it wasn’t until Druckmüller entered the picture that they were able to develop the gear and the mathematical techniques to do it.

With just a minute to go to totality, the researchers begin removing protective filters from the lenses. It’s 50 minutes to sunset, and the waning sun has just begun to light up the clouds above the horizon with the first tinge of orange. Then, suddenly, the evening begins a rapid and premature descent into darkness. Along the edge of the fantastically thin solar crescent, the brilliant orange points known as Baily’s Beads flash and disappear—the last fragments of photospheric light visible through deep lunar valleys. As totality begins, observers remove their glasses. The hot air cools. The graduate students remain quietly and intently focused on their gear.

Druckmüller looks up from his camera toward the darkened plains. Around the blackened solar disk rises the magnificent golden halo of the corona. In the hush on the mountainside, it seems that even the birds have gone still. The sky is ablaze with fiery colors all along the horizon where the deep lunar shadow drops off. Venus burns brilliantly in the southwest, a sharp white pinpoint in the darkened sky. The sound of camera shutters suddenly fills the air. Then, as quickly as it fell, the darkness begins to recede, bid farewell with another handful of golden Baily’s Beads.

The crowd erupts in cheers. The Ph.D. students throw themselves at each other and hug like they mean it.

“The students did most of the work this time, so I actually allowed myself to really look at it,” Druckmüller says. “It was beautiful. Pico Trigaza may not have been the best for science photography, but from the aesthetic point of view, it was extraordinary.”

The 2026 solar-eclipse team at Pico Trigaza in Spain included [from left] Magdalena Šrotířová, Peter Urgoš, Martin Fornůsek, Miloslav Druckmüller, Václav Široký, and Martin Šebek.Václav Široký

But for Druckmüller, this is just the beginning. While other eclipse chasers will race to release their images, he will take his time. He expects to publish the first visible-light images of the corona in about two weeks. Processing the iron-ion images, and uncovering whatever insights they may hold, will take months—maybe even a whole year.

“Probably until the next eclipse in 2027” in North Africa, Druckmüller says.

Who knows? Maybe he’ll even enjoy that one, too.

Tereza Pultarova is a London-based journalist specializing in aerospace and defense technologies. She is a native of the Czech Republic.

I enjoyed this piece very, very much, and I truly hope this team continues its work.

Those are some pretty impressive photos! It also seems like the iron ion filtering is pretty unique. I love seeing cases where people build something they want to see in the world with minimal outside support. Seems like it would be a solid return on more public money to seek out and support scrappy projects like this one.

#3230. Global Roller Derby League Eyes 2027 Launch, Aims to Update the Sport for Modern TV Audiences (EXCLUSIVE)

Former blockchain executive David Berns, who served as president and chief operating officer of Blockchains, LLC, and also helped create the digital media platform ETHNews, is doing something entirely different for his next project: Roller derby.

Berns has been named CEO of Global Roller Derby League, which is looking to revive the sport for TV audiences when it launches next year. GRDL is run by Berns, along with “Broadway” Danny Wolf, president of league operations; Elie Dekel, president of GRDL brands; and Dave Harding, executive in charge of production. Related Stories 'Heartland' Review: Jessica Chastain Rocks a Stetson and a Swagger for a Soapy Nashville Noir 'The Diplomat,' 'Nobody Wants This,' 'East of Eden' Among Series to Take Part in Netflix's 'FYSee: The Fall Edit' Awards Showcase (EXCLUSIVE)

“Roller derby has a remarkable history and an enduring appeal,” Berns said in a statement. “We see an opportunity to reintroduce this iconic sport, a classic piece of Americana, with an entirely new approach. We combine the athleticism and excitement of a sports competition with the personalities, rivalries and storytelling that today’s audiences expect. The Global Roller Derby League is building a powerful brand that we believe fans will embrace well beyond game day.”

Roller derby remains a popular pastime; in Los Angeles, outfits including Angel City Derby, Derby Dolls, SFV Roller Derby and Los Anarchists Junior Derby draw plenty of interest.

GRDL is hoping to take that one step closer and make roller derby the kind of draw it once was during the early days of television. The sports entertainment property is planning to recruit male and female skaters from around the world to compete on five co-ed teams representing New York, Los Angeles, Chicago, Dallas and Miami. GRDL hopes to attract a wide range of demos with its weekly televised games, which will take place in front of live fans.

“Roller derby has always had something special — it’s fast, physical, unpredictable and filled with personalities you don’t see in other sports. I’ve spent much of my career around this sport, and I know firsthand what makes it so exciting for fans of all ages,” Wolf said in a statement. “What we’re building with GRDL respects that history while introducing a new generation to the energy, competition and larger-than-life characters that make roller derby so unique.”

The GRDL plans to hold open auditions for participants in early 2027, and it’s pitching the franchise to potential broadcast and streaming partners.

Berns’ past credits also include serving as chief financial officer of blockchain software developer Berns Inc. He was also a business litigation and international commercial attorney, and later a partner at Berns Weiss LLP.

Wolf has a professional wrestling and roller derby background, and served as the TV voice of roller derby franchises the Los Angeles T-Birds and San Francisco Bay Bombers. He was the on-air host and a writer for TNN’s “RollerJam” and is known for bringing Memphis’s Continental Wrestling Association to cable.

Dekel’s entertainment branding, marketing, merchandising and gaming experience includes Fox Entertainment, Legendary Pictures, Saban Brands and more, working on brands such as “The Simpsons” and “Mighty Morphin Power Rangers.”

Harding is an Emmy Award-winning producer (“Wage Slaves: Not Getting By in America”) and has worked on projects such as the Academy Award-nominated “Encounters At The End of the World” and the feature documentaries “Grizzly Man” and “Chasing Trane.”
