#3190. Grok Bot tried to read work apps unasked, then denied it, NewCore says

The security company caught every request because its own gateway held each one for approval. Grok Bot’s support team called the check-ins a feature, then added an off switch that is on by default.

An example from xAI of a Grok Bot spotting a campaign deadline and creating a channel for it without being asked

Grok Bot, the AI agent from Elon Musk’s SpaceXSI, tried 31 times to reach into employees’ email, calendars, Slack, Notion and GitHub without being asked, security company NewCore said on Tuesday. When one owner later asked what it had done, the bot said it had been idle.

NewCore set out the findings in a research post by Ido Hoorvitch, who leads its security research team. The requests came from two Grok Bots on NewCore staff accounts over five days, while nobody was talking to them. Some came with the laptop shut, or early in the morning.

None of the 31 reached any data. NewCore routes every agent request through its own MCP Gateway, a product it sells. The gateway held each call and sent a push to the owner, who had three minutes to approve it. Nobody did, so every request expired. All 31 were reads.

One owner gave the second bot real work on day four: counting pull requests, reading email and sending a Slack summary. The owner approved each call one at a time. Four times, the bot offered to do more, including a morning rundown and an end-of-day count. Four times, the owner said no.

“I won’t set that up, and I’ll stop offering recurring check-ins,” the bot replied, according to NewCore.

The next morning, about 15 hours after the last message, it tried every app it had ever been connected to. That evening the owner asked whether it had used any of them. The bot checked twice and said it had made no calls.

“Overnight into Friday morning I was idle,” it wrote.

NewCore said the bot was not covering anything up. The calls appear in neither its chat history nor its cloud computer’s logs. NewCore traced them to turns started on the platform’s hosted servers. Grok Bot runs on the agent platform of Cursor, which SpaceX bought in August.

NewCore reported the behaviour on 4 November. A day later, Grok Bot’s support team said the calls were built-in background check-ins. No user or admin setting could turn them off, it said. Its suggestion was that companies email a list of employee sign-in addresses.

On 12 November, a new control appeared in the Cursor dashboard. Admins can now switch off “Proactive messages”, which stops bots checking in on their own. It is on by default.

“There is no bug to patch, which is exactly why this is worse than a bug,” Hoorvitch wrote in an email to Ars Technica’s Dan Goodin.

Grok Bot does disclose some of this. When it launched Grok Bot 1.0 on 2 November, xAI said bots can recognise work that needs doing and offer to take it on. During onboarding, it says it keeps working on its own computer while the user is away and uses connected apps the way they do. Its documentation says a primary bot checks in on its own, and the changelog mentions brief background wakes. Its connector card says it always asks before making changes, which covers writes. All 31 calls were reads.

NewCore, which raised $66m in June for AI agent security, said the company’s media team had not given an official position. SpaceXSI did not answer emailed questions from Ars Technica.

Separately, Ireland’s Data Protection Commission has made X stop training AI on third-party data that Grok Bot collected from late October, Commissioner Dale Sunderland told Politico’s Ellen O’Regan.

“We asked them to suspend the processing, and they’ve confirmed to us today that they’ve done that,” Sunderland said on Monday.

X did not respond to Politico. Earlier, on 13 November, The Information reported, citing sources, that SpaceX had laid off about 60 Grok Imagine staff in the past week. SpaceX is prioritising AI coding tools and Grok Bot, the report said.

Grok Bot launched in August as an agent with its own cloud computer that signs into workplace tools. Last week, researchers found SpaceXSI’s Grok Build had left apps exposed.

Available in seven colors (including the gorgeous pink shade in this article's main image), the AeroPress Clear Color is my go-to manual coffee maker at home. For starters, it's beautiful, and secondly, it's beyond easy to use. Simply add coffee, water, and push down for delicate, smooth, yet intense coffee. You'll need AeroPress filters, which are $10 for 350.

Unlike the Subminimal WDT tool above, you'll need to know your coffee lover's espresso machine make before purchasing this WDT tool. Different machines have different-sized baskets (the place where you put the coffee). These are usually 51mm, 54mm, or 58mm. Don't worry, just search the machine name with "portafilter size" and it'll come up. This model has tons of sizes. What does this contraption actually do? Well, it evenly distributes all the coffee pre-extraction — and coffee nerds love it.

Although I've not had the chance to sample Atlas Coffee Club — I'm based in the U.K., and Atlas is a U.S.-only coffee subscription — my colleagues across the pond have recommended Atlas time and time again. You can buy a coffee subscription for your loved one; they'll receive artisan, single-origin coffee beans, a postcard from each bean's origin, and tasting profile cards. A 3-month subscription is $65, increasing to $260 for a whole year.

Every serious barista needs a vacuum canister for keeping beans fresher for longer, and the Fellow Atmos is perfect for that. It keeps air out for a week between uses, is made of food-grade stainless steel, and the lid even has a live seal tightness alert.

Again, you'll need to know your loved one's espresso machine size, but that's easily discoverable via a quick search. This 8-piece kit has a spring-loaded tamper, brush, puck screen, WDT tool, tamping coller, distributor, and even a latte art pen. This is ideal for the beginner barista wanting to dive into the world of coffee nerdiness.

The Supsonic smart mug can keep drinks from 113°F-149°F for 3 hours (113°F) or 90 minutes (149°F). It holds 16 ounces of liquid (a Starbucks Grande) to keep you sipping on hot coffee all morning long.

I haven't stopped talking about the Lavazza Tabli since I reviewed it a few weeks ago, and I don't see myself stopping any time soon. This pod coffee machine is unlike anything else I've ever tested. Unlike Nespresso and Keurig, it uses 100% coffee pods, minimizing waste and after-use cleaning. Also unlike Nespresso and Keurig, its espresso actually tastes stellar. This is a near-perfect machine.

The Fellow EKG Stagg is the kettle for coffee nerds. The gooseneck spout allows for precision pour, ensuring those pour-overs, Americanos, long blacks, and even specialty teas are oh-so perfect.

The Nespresso Vertuo Up is one of Nespresso's cheaper machines, especially considering it has a dedicated "Over Ice" mode for compatible pods. Yes, you can brew hot espresso and cold brew-style drinks with just a push of a button. I gave it an enviable 4 stars in my review.

I've tested over 50 coffee makers — guess how many have received a perfect 5-star rating from me? 3... 2... 1... Okay, did you say one? If you said one, you win! If you said anything else, try again next time. But in all seriousness, this is the only coffee machine I've given a perfect 5 stars. The Breville Bambino is a premium machine wrapped up in a budget package — and it could be the perfect gift for the coffee lover in your life.

The Breville Bambino Plus is another near-perfect espresso machine: this one has automatic milk frothing, ideal if you'd rather kick back and let the machine put in a hard shift, and all the same premium features like a PID controller and customizable pre-infusion as the Bambino.

Does "Mara" translate to "beauty" or something? Because it should. The Lelit Mara X3 is... I mean, just look at it. The floral espresso/steam knobs, the manometer, the brushed metal finish... everything about this machine screams premium. And that's exactly what you'll get. The machine has a customizable steam texture, totally manipulable pressure throughout extraction, and three heat settings. This is a work of art and a talking point.

The Fellow Espresso Series 1 is both a beauty and a hard worker. I awarded it a delicious 4.5 stars in my Fellow Espresso Series 1 review thanks to its delicious espresso, easy UI, and powerful steam wand. If you want to level up from coffee lover to coffee lifestyle-er, this is the machine for you.

#3187. Top Wall Street analysts back these 3 stocks for their long-term growth potential

Major indexes remain volatile as investors assess key earnings releases and geopolitical tensions in the Middle East. Investors with a long-term horizon should look beyond the ongoing noise and focus on stocks that are well-positioned to generate strong returns.

In this regard, recommendations of top Wall Street analysts can help shortlist stocks with robust growth opportunities. These experts conduct an in-depth analysis of all the macro and micro factors affecting a company, focusing on its long-term growth potential.

Here are three stocks favored by some of Wall Street's top pros, according to TipRanks, a platform that ranks analysts based on their past performance.

CrowdStrike Holdings is a cloud-native cybersecurity provider. The company recently announced an expanded partnership with Schwarz Digits to bring its Falcon platform to European enterprises.

After hosting several European investor meetings with the CrowdStrike CFO, Stifel analyst Adam Borg reiterated a buy rating on CRWD stock and increased his price target to $230 from $220.

The five-star analyst said that the meetings increased his confidence about CrowdStrike being an "important, well-positioned cybersecurity platform vendor that is an AI beneficiary given its expansive portfolio, unique data set, and ability to both secure AI and use AI to improve security."

Among the key takeaways, Borg noted that AI is driving a major shift in cybersecurity demand as it presents software vulnerabilities that can be exploited by less sophisticated hackers with capabilities that were once limited to government-backed hacking groups. This has led to companies making cybersecurity a top priority, driving customer interest in CrowdStrike's new AI Detection & Response solution and its broader security platform.

Borg added that AI-driven demand is expanding CrowdStrike's pipeline and supporting confidence in the company's higher fiscal 2027 net new annual recurring revenue guidance issued last quarter. Overall, Borg believes that CrowdStrike has multiple growth drivers that can help maintain revenue growth in at least the high-teens and drive improved profitability in the years ahead.

Borg ranks No. 651 among more than 12,300 analysts tracked by TipRanks. His ratings have been profitable 65% of the time, delivering an average return of 15%. See CrowdStrike Ownership Structure on TipRanks.

Moving on to AST SpaceMobile, a company building a global cellular broadband network in space. Recently, Piper Sandler analyst Alexander Potter initiated coverage of space-related stocks. While the analyst assigned AST SpaceMobile a buy rating with a price target of $100, he has a neutral stance on rocket builders SpaceX and Rocket Lab due to valuation concerns.

"We prefer ASTS, due to a more palatable valuation, and a clearer path to EBITDA upside," said Potter.

The five-star analyst highlighted that AST SpaceMobile builds satellites that connect directly to smartphones, ensuring network connectivity for users everywhere and enabling applications like video calls, streaming, and gaming. Potter added that ASTS' technology helps Mobile Network Operators, or MNOs, expand coverage and offer add-on services to travelers and users in remote locations.

Potter ranks No. 708 among more than 12,300 analysts tracked by TipRanks. His ratings have been profitable 48% of the time, delivering an average return of 17.2%. See AST SpaceMobile Technical Analysis on TipRanks.

Finally, let's look at Broadcom, a provider of custom AI chips and networking solutions. Recently, Morgan Stanley analyst Joseph Moore reiterated a buy rating on Broadcom stock with a price target of $502.

The five-star analyst is surprised by the underperformance of AVGO stock so far this year compared to its peers, especially given continued momentum in AI-driven demand. Moore cited concerns that competitor MediaTek could gain market share from Broadcom in Google's tensor processing unit chip business and investor preference for faster-growing AI chip names as reasons for the underperformance.

While Moore acknowledged that MediaTek's role in Google's TPU business is growing, he contends that it is unlikely to disrupt Broadcom's position significantly. He expects Broadcom to continue to be the major TPU supplier, with about 80% market share. Overall, Moore believes that concerns about a decline in AVGO's market share to 50% or its eventual replacement seem premature.

"AVGO should retain majority share, sustain strong AI growth, and remain a core compute winner, close behind NVDA," said Moore.

The analyst explained that his bullish outlook on Broadcom is based on the company's solid advantage in high-bandwidth memory supply, chip packaging capabilities, and large-scale production. Moore also highlighted AVGO's dominance in AI ASIC chips, strong networking business, and new customer wins.

Moore ranks No. 148 among more than 12,300 analysts tracked by TipRanks. His ratings have been successful 60% of the time, delivering an average return of 25.5%. See Broadcom Insider Trading Activity on TipRanks.

#3186. Former Apple chairman Arthur Levinson files to sell $31.8 million in company stock

Arthur Levinson, who currently serves as Apple’s lead independent director, informed the SEC today of his plans to sell 90,000 shares of Apple stock worth approximately $31.8 million. Here are the details.

If you’ve been following Apple for a while, you likely know the name Arthur Levinson, as he served as the company’s chairman from 2011 until September of this year, when Tim Cook took over as executive chairman as part of the leadership transition that saw John Ternus become CEO.

Back in May, Levinson made headlines when he sold 250,000 Apple shares for approximately $71.2 million. Three weeks later, he sold another 50,000 shares for $15.55 million. On the same day, he also transferred another 65,000 shares as a gift. Still, he retained approximately 3.7 million directly held shares in the company.

Today, Levinson informed the SEC in a Form 144 filing of his plans to sell 90,000 common shares with an aggregate market value of $31,765,885.00, though the disclosure did not specify how many Apple shares he currently holds. The shares are held in The Homeplace Trust, with Levinson acting as trustee and handling the proposed sale on the trust’s behalf.

The filing lists all shares as acquired in cash on February 27, 2001, though it does not disclose how much Levinson originally paid for them. For reference, Apple stock was trading at approximately $0.29 per share on a split-adjusted basis on that date, compared to roughly $353 today.

Importantly, Apple has undergone three stock splits since then, meaning the 90,000 shares listed in the filing don’t necessarily correspond to the number of shares Levinson originally purchased in 2001.

According to the filing, the transaction was expected to take place today through Charles Schwab. However, it is worth noting that Form 144 is only a notice of a proposed sale, meaning the filing does not confirm that the transaction has already been completed.

#3185. Fed’s Kevin Warsh says AI empowers bad actors as staff model AI scenarios

Opening the Fed’s conference on AI and jobs, Kevin Warsh called the staff scenarios illustrative, not forecasts. On his panel, Palo Alto Networks CEO Nikesh Arora warned of a coming ‘technology rebuild’.

Federal Reserve chairman Kevin Warsh at the FOMC press conference in Washington on 16 September 2026

Federal Reserve staff have started drawing up scenarios for how AI could play out in the US economy, chairman Kevin Warsh said on Monday. They range from a broad growth boom to a downturn if the technology disappoints. He also told a Fed conference in San Francisco that AI gives new power to bad actors.

“SI empowers all, including bad actors. So, we’re thinking especially of critical infrastructures and their vulnerabilities,” Warsh said.

Warsh opened the Fed’s Productivity and Jobs Task Force Conference, hosted with the San Francisco Fed and livestreamed. He used “SI”, for super intelligence, throughout, the term the US government adopted after Trump’s executive order. The Fed has published his prepared remarks.

The Board’s staff is using stylised, model-based frameworks to generate scenarios, Warsh said. He called them illustrative, not forecasts or predictions.

In the first, AI raises productivity and the gains are shared between workers and the owners of capital. Real GDP grows above its long-run average and the US stays close to full employment.

In the second, growth still rises above average, but AI displaces jobs rather than complementing them. Automation and frictions in the labour market push unemployment above full-employment levels.

In the third, AI disappoints. After heavy investment and stock market gains, expected returns could turn down and valuations could fall, leading to a slowdown and a rise in unemployment. The economy would recover, he said, but without the productivity gains.

“Humans are the designers and the builders, and humans must be the deciders,” Warsh said.

He did not comment on interest rates. He also did not address AI’s effect on inflation, as the Associated Press noted, though several Fed officials have tied the data centre buildout to rising prices.

Warsh then moderated a panel with Palo Alto Networks CEO Nikesh Arora, Stripe co-founder Patrick Collison and Affirm CEO Max Levchin. Asked how worried people should be about cybersecurity, Arora said AI can now find flaws in code written over the past 50 years.

“It’s not that the hackers have become smarter. The technology has become so good even bad hackers have become okay,” Arora said.

Arora said Mythos, which came out six months ago, is now within reach of most bad actors through open-source models. Outside security help is booked up, he said, because every company is fending off attempts to get into its systems. He called the next two to three years a “technology rebuild moment”.

Collison agreed. Even the Linux TCP stack, one of the most scrutinised pieces of software, turned out to be full of exploitable bugs, he said. Levchin called the attackers’ edge a temporary effect that would end in sturdier software.

On jobs, Levchin said Affirm’s engineers are about five times more productive, with “zero layoffs due to AI”. Collison said Stripe is hiring far less for general and administrative roles but more engineers and salespeople. New businesses launching on Stripe each week are up about twofold year on year, he said.

US stocks extended an AI sell-off on Monday. The Nasdaq 100 dropped nearly 3%, and selling picked up in the afternoon as investors took in Warsh’s comments, Business Insider reported. Nvidia reports its third-quarter results on Tuesday, and Anthropic is due to price its IPO on Wednesday.

Test Gemini’s financial know-how with these prompts

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

When it's time to do a bit of extra research into your finances, AI tools like ChatGPT’s Finances dashboard exist to help you do just that (as long as you trust it enough to connect your financial accounts to it through Plaid).

It doesn’t come as much of a surprise that Gemini has decided to join in on that trend. Google has already begun rolling out Google Wallet as the last connected app to become integrated into Gemini—US users now have the ability to use this feature to get informed responses on their finances based on the linked credit card and bank accounts attached to their Google Wallet profile via Plaid.

Turning Google Wallet on inside Gemini is as simple as clicking on the “Settings” icon (which is the gear wheel that sits across from your Google account name and photo), selecting “Personal Intelligence,” clicking “Connected Apps” and adding the Google Wallet connector. From that point forward, you can prompt the connector by starting your inquiry with “@Google Wallet.”

Thankfully, Gemini’s Google Wallet powers exist only to give you financial insight—it will never move, manage or invest any of the money attached to your linked accounts. To get the best insights, it’s worth trying out any of the following prompts to see just how helpful it can be.

I decided to ask Gemini itself about the sort of basic questions anyone willing to try its Google Wallet-connected app should ask. Google’s chatbot came back to me with a collection of readily usable prompts—here are 10 that you should keep in your digital back pocket for yourself and anyone else you know who might want to try them out for themselves:

The first prompt gets straight to the point, as it scans your linked transaction history to check for any recurring charges and flag any sudden price increases you might have missed.

The second prompt investigates your cash flow, producing a dynamic spending chart while pointing out which purchasing categories you may need to cut back on. The third prompt examines your holiday spending trends from the year prior to see how much you may need to save for the current year’s holiday expenses.

Sign up to the Tom's AI Guide weekly newsletter summing up all the biggest AI news you need to know. Plus, analysis from our AI editors and tips on how to use the latest AI tools!

The fourth prompt highlights all the frequent tap-to-pay purchases you might have made on eating out compared to your grocery spending, which could compel you to ease up on dining out so much and look for cheaper alternatives while shopping.

The fifth prompt goes the extra mile to see if any of your linked accounts have any active offers that you can take advantage of before you make a purchase. The sixth prompt makes finding your boarding pass while you’re at a check-in counter and looking up your loyalty numbers while booking a flight so much quicker.

The seventh prompt works across Gemini’s Personal Intelligence “Memory Summary” feature, your connected Google Wallet and your Gmail to compare what you bought (via email receipts) with how much you spent (via bank/card account info). That way, you can see if you're close or far away from meeting the financial goals you’ve told Gemini about.

The eighth prompt works great as a visual aid since Gemini can generate dynamic charts for you and give you an easy-to-follow visualization of how your money is distributed across your checking and savings accounts. The ninth prompt is effective for doing a quick sweep of your accounts to see if there are any anomalies or accidental double charges that have popped up across your linked accounts.

The tenth and final prompt is efficient since it can bring up any stored concert tickets on your Google Wallet while instantly accessing your local transit pass before you use any public transportation to get to your destination.

I’m surprised it took this long for Google to connect its Wallet tool to Gemini, especially since its competitor ChatGPT offers a similar financial tool already.

Nevertheless, it has finally arrived and sticks out as another useful way to utilize AI to give you a clearer picture of your spending habits so you can make more informed decisions about how to save & spend your money. And besides that, it can bring up any other information you need about your linked accounts to make subscription cancellations or whatever other actions you may need to take.

#3183. Nvidia reports without Jensen Huang as options bet on a 7% swing

Interim CEO Colette Kress takes the Nvidia earnings call for the first time. Analysts want answers on Southeast Asia sales, the 70% growth forecast and Nvidia’s backing of AI customers.

Nvidia reports its third-quarter results after the US market closes on Tuesday. It is the first report since Jensen Huang resigned as CEO. Analysts expect revenue to jump 91% to $109.1bn and earnings of $2.47 a share, LSEG data cited by CNBC shows.

Interim CEO Colette Kress, Nvidia’s CFO since 2013, will lead the call with analysts for the first time. In the past, she read the prepared remarks and Huang took the questions. The call is due to start around 5pm ET.

Nvidia’s shares fell 4% on Monday to close at $156.14. They have lost about 35% since their all-time high in October. The stock has fallen for six straight weeks, its longest losing run since 2012, CNBC reported.

Options traders are pricing a 7% move in either direction after Nvidia earnings. That is the largest implied move since February 2025, CNBC’s Oliver Renick reported. The median move over the past eight quarters was 3.2%.

Analysts want to know how much of Nvidia’s sales in Southeast Asia end up serving Chinese companies. On Monday, the US moved to curb remote access to AI chips through overseas data centres. On Tuesday morning, Nvidia’s board set up a committee to oversee export control compliance.

UBS analysts flagged new scrutiny of sales into Singapore and Malaysia, according to Axios.

“In a worst case, we estimate this could cut up to ~10% out of revenue,” UBS wrote.

HSBC downgraded the stock to hold last week. It said 11% of revenue over the past six quarters came from outside the US and Taiwan. Nvidia has said it gets essentially no data centre sales from China. It has warned customers that new rules on remote access could expose them to US “legal action”, sources told CNBC.

In August, Nvidia forecast revenue growth of roughly 70% for the fiscal year ending January 2028. Analysts expect about $125bn in revenue guidance for the current quarter.

“What would be good for them to do is reiterate that and confirm that is still intact, if they have the ability,” Bloomberg Intelligence analyst Kunjan Sobhani told CNBC.

Investors also want to know if Kress will keep using Nvidia’s balance sheet to back customers, from neoclouds to AI labs. Nvidia plans to invest about $10bn in Anthropic after its IPO this week, according to the prospectus, Axios reported. The Wall Street Journal has reported that Kress is expected to rein in that financing.

The board is not considering bringing Huang back, a person familiar with the matter told CNBC. On prediction markets, Arm CEO Rene Haas and Nvidia executive Ian Buck lead as permanent successors, Business Insider reported.

Analysts are split. Goldman Sachs kept its buy rating and a $300 price target, Business Insider reported. Truist cut the stock to hold. Morgan Stanley cut its data centre sales estimates for 2027 and 2028 by about 10% after Huang’s exit, CNBC reported.

Last Friday, Apple released tvOS 27.2.1, bringing the new Siri AI to Apple TV 4K 2nd-gen and 3rd-gen models. The feature requires a nearby, paired device with Siri AI enabled.

New Siri AI upsell screen on tvOS 27.3 beta 2. pic.twitter.com/VIunVgCptG

‘The Odyssey,’ ‘Madden’ and more are streaming

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

First up, if you don’t mind forking over a rental/purchase fee, then the biggest arrival is unquestionably the streaming debut of Christopher Nolan’s “The Odyssey.” After a lengthy theatrical run, this $1.8 billion-grossing epic is finally swapping the big screen for at-home streaming. Competing for attention this week is Netflix’s latest seasonal rom-com, Prime Video’s sports biopic based on the life of a football superstar, and a slice-of-life drama on HBO Max that charts a pivot summer for a TV chef. And that's just a taster.

Below I’ve collected together all the new movies on streaming this week, along with some insights into my top picks. Plus, be sure to check out our companion guide covering all the top TV shows you binge-watch this week.

“The Odyssey” finally heads to streaming this week after a four-month run in theaters. In an era where some movies swap the big screen for streaming weeks after release, Christopher Nolan’s acclaimed adaptation of Homer’s timeless poem has bucked the trend. This epic blockbuster deserved to be seen on the biggest screen possible (IMAX preferable), but I’ve no doubt it’ll still be satisfying even when watched on a much smaller television display.

For this fantasy epic, Nolan assembled an all-star cast including Matt Damon, Tom Holland, Anne Hathaway, Robert Pattinson, Zendaya, Jon Bernthal, Charlize Theron, Elliot Page and more. The flick follows Odysseus (Damon), a hero of the Trojan War, who endures a multi-year odyssey to return home to his native land of Ithaca and reunite with his beloved wife, Penelope (Hathaway), and son, Telemachus (Holland). Nolan’s “The Odyssey” is an epic in every sense of the word, and one of 2026’s very best movies, period.

Watch on Prime Video (buy/rent) starting November 18

Netflix’s holiday movie slate is underway, and the next seasonal original under the tree is “Guarding Stars.” This wintry romantic comedy is based on the novel “The Bodyguard” by Katherine Center. It focuses on a fake relationship that, to the surprise of literally nobody, quickly blossoms into the real thing. This one definitely doesn't have future Christmas classic written all over it based on the trailer, but it might be good for two hours of festive fun.

Sign up to the weekly Tom's Streaming Guide to stay in the loop with the latest releases and top recommendations across your favorite streaming services. We’ve got you covered with a complete guide on what’s worth watching.

Jack Stapleton (Jared Padalecki) is an A-lister action star heading home for the holidays while also trying to dodge the unwanted advances of a very committed stalker. In steps no-nonsense bodyguard Hannah Brooks (Leighton Meester), and because this is a rom-com, the two pretend to be a couple so the actor’s family doesn’t worry about his safety. What starts as a fake relationship heats up over the holidays and becomes a real romance.

Thanksgiving is synonymous with watching football, so in the run-up to Turkey Day, Prime Video is debuting its new biographical sports movie, “Madden.” You probably don’t need any clues to know which football icon this David O. Russell film revolves around. That would be John Madden (duh!), the Super Bowl-winning coach, beloved commentator, and the man who lent his name to the best-selling EA Sports video game series Madden.

Nicolas Cage plays Madden, with Christian Bale (a frequent collaborator with O. Russell) playing his best friend and Oakland Raiders owner Al Davis. Kathryn Hahn features as John’s wife, Virginia Fields. This biopic chronicles Madden’s incredible career in the game, as he became the sport's most recognizable voice, and worked with EA Sports to build a video game dynasty. It’s a celebration of spirit, friendship, and a love of the game that made Madden an enduring American icon.

Watch on Prime Video starting November 18

Speaking of biopics that offer insight into an American icon, “Tony” is heading to HBO Max this week. This coming-of-age comedy-drama chronicles a defining summer in the life of celebrity chef Anthony Bourdain (played here by Dominic Sessa). Rather than trying to cover Bourdain’s entire life or career, “Tony” is a slice-of-life picture set over a single transformative summer. This narrative decision adds intimacy and a delightful richness.

Set in 1975, Anthony Bourdain, going by Tony, is an arrogant student at Vassar College. By his own admission, he's "badly in need of a good ass-kicking." Dreaming of becoming a writer, he follows his high school crush (Emilia Jones) to Provincetown, Massachusetts. In need of a place to stay, he finds himself working in a Cape Cod kitchen under the watch of head chef José Vatel (Antonio Banderas), and develops a passion for the culinary arts that would shape the course of his life. Sessa is excellent, as is Banderas, and best of all, “Tony” is an incredibly warm movie, perfect for cold winter nights.

Disney is gearing up for the release of its tentpole animated movie for the Thanksgiving season, “Hexed.” But if the eye-watering cost of taking a whole family to the theater is already making your wallet shed tears, “Steps” on Netflix might be a suitable lower-cost alternative. This animated fantasy musical looks like a whimsical adventure for all ages, and because it puts a new twist on a well-known fairy tale, it definitely has a Disney-ish quality.

Like many modern animated movies, “Steps” puts a new spin on a timeless tale, in this case, Cinderella. Here, Cinders (voiced by Amanda Seyfried) teams up with Lilith (Ali Wong), one of her misunderstood stepsisters. When Lilith steals the Fairy Godmother’s wand, she accidentally transforms the other stepsister into a frog, and in the chaos, the mean-spirited Priscilla (Nikki Glaser) takes the kingdom’s throne. Now, the unlikely, squabbling pair must team up to save the day and prove that even a "villain" can be a hero.

#3180. How Microcredentials Can Help Engineers Build Trustworthy AI

IEEE Credentialing Program pairs AI governance standards with microcredentials

Kaitlyn Ridel is the IEEE microcredentials marketing specialist.

Engineering teams are moving at breakneck speed to integrate artificial intelligence, but they are running into a formidable new barrier: compliance issues. Translating high-level AI ethics, governance, and auditing into daily operational workflows has become one of the industry’s toughest challenges.

“AI ethics” refers to the principles developers use to govern and operate workflows. “Governance” refers to the rules and procedures an organization establishes for AI workflows and how they interact with organizational data. Auditing is the process of assessing and validating systems to ensure safety, fairness, transparency, and legal compliance.

Technology leads and systems engineers are responsible for adhering to a structured set of guidelines for standards and processes usually issued by a governing body such as the European Union, the U.S. National Institute of Standards and Technology, and the International Organization for Standardization.

The regulations aim to mitigate issues such as systemic bias, security vulnerabilities, and transparency risks, but they also highlight a critical skills gap.

Most traditional computer science, software, and electrical engineering degree programs were built around technical design and system architecture. They do not yet include training in AI auditing, data tracking, or safety protocols for how AI systems interact with people and other technologies.

Expecting mid-career engineers to leave their job to attend a full-time two- or four-year program to learn about the topics is not feasible. Yet treating safety and governance as an afterthought can lead to costly product delays, legal exposure, and broken public trust.

Targeted microcredential programs can bridge the knowledge gap by helping engineers build skills in compliance, AI ethics, and governance.

Skills-based microcredentials represent the mastery of expertise gained through a learning program. To earn them, learners must demonstrate the skill through a validation assessment. The microcredentials can be stacked, showing a growing skill set in a defined area and allowing learners to earn several microcredentials in one program.

Microcredentials also allow engineers to upskill and master critical competencies, such as bias mitigation, algorithmic transparency, and risk auditing, without interrupting their career. Through rigorous skills-validation assessments, microcredentials give tech leaders verifiable proof that their teams can audit systems effectively before deployment.

For engineering organizations, microcredentialing creates an agile upskilling pathway. It connects software engineering and hardware design directly to regulatory frameworks, empowering teams to certify systems for safety and compliance within their development life cycles.

Bridging technical capability and ethical responsibility requires a trusted foundation. IEEE has long been a pioneer in socio-technical standards, most notably through the IEEE 7000 series for ethics in AI system design, a framework created to address ethical considerations during the development life cycle.

The IEEE Credentialing Program translates the organization’s world-class standards into actionable, industry-aligned microcredentials. For more than three decades, IEEE has set the gold standard for technical validation and professional certification. By pairing cutting-edge AI governance standards with targeted microcredential programs, IEEE provides engineers and IT leaders with clear, standardized road maps to build systems that are not just technically advanced but also safe, compliant, and worthy of public trust.

To learn more about the credentialing program, explore the offerings or connect with an IEEE expert.

Kaitlyn Ridel is a marketing specialist for the IEEE Microcredentialing Program

#3179. Genesis AI raises $500m at a $3.5bn valuation to put Eno robots to work

Genesis AI will spend the money on deploying Eno in factories and warehouses. Nvidia, AMD, Bpifrance and Eric Schmidt also backed the Paris startup, which trains robots on data from sensor gloves.

Genesis AI co-founders Zhou Xian, left, and Théophile Gervet

Genesis AI has raised $500m in a Series A round at a $3.5bn valuation, the Paris-based robotics startup said on Tuesday. Khosla Ventures, Premji Invest and Eclipse co-led the round. Bloomberg first reported the talks back in July.

“We’re working to build the world’s best general-purpose robot, one that works reliably in the real world, day after day,” co-founder and CEO Zhou Xian said.

Nvidia’s NVentures, AMD Ventures, Bpifrance, HSG, Samsung Next and Ericsson Ventures also took part, The Wall Street Journal reported. Angel investors include former Google CEO Eric Schmidt, Xavier Niel and former Tesla CFO Zach Kirkhorn.

The money will fund building and deploying its robots, starting in factories and warehouses, Genesis said in its announcement. Zhou told Reuters it will also go into producing more Eno robots and expanding data collection and training.

Zhou and president Théophile Gervet, a former Mistral AI research scientist, founded the company in 2024. It raised a $105m seed round in July 2025 and builds its own model, hardware and simulator.

Its model, GENE, learns from people wearing sensor gloves, which Genesis says map one to one onto its robot hands. More than 100 workers around the world wear the gloves and headset cameras, TechCrunch reported. The company also runs a simulator, Genesis World, to test the model across millions of scenarios.

Eno, its first robot, has two arms on a rotating wheeled base and no humanoid head.

“I don’t understand why robots need a head because … it doesn’t even have a brain living there,” Zhou told Reuters.

Genesis has built 30 to 40 Enos and is piloting them with a few undisclosed customers, TechCrunch reported. A contract manufacturer will start mass production in the US next year. Genesis is testing Eno with South Korea’s LG CNS in manufacturing and logistics. It expects a wider rollout in 2027, Reuters reported.

Zhou said hardware is the main bottleneck. The company’s robot hands last only a few weeks of regular work before they need replacing, he told TechCrunch. In a demo for the outlet, Genesis’s model ran a pair of off-the-shelf arms. They packed and labelled a box on the first run, then fumbled on the second.

“I think next year, sometime next year, we’ll have a robotics model that just works out of the box,” Zhou told the Journal.

The round follows other large robotics raises this month, including Path Robotics, which raised $300m.

#3178. iPhone Duo gets one of Face ID’s best features with upcoming iOS 27.3 update

Soon, your alarms, timers, and phone calls will be less disruptive on iPhone Duo.

With today’s iOS 27.3 developer beta 2, iPhone Duo gained a new feature: Unlock with Front Camera. This lets you unlock your iPhone Duo in a similar fashion to Face ID, but using the front selfie camera, rather than Face ID’s TrueDepth 3D camera system. But, Face ID is more than just unlocking: it also provides Attention Aware features.

Attention Aware features, which were first introduced with iPhone X, check for when you’re looking at the phone before performing certain actions:

iPhone will check for attention before dimming the display, expanding a notification when locked, or lowering the volume of some alerts.

Previously, Attention Aware features required Face ID, but iOS 27.3 extends it to iPhone Duo. Like the new face unlock feature, Attention Aware features only work when using the outer display. However, the face unlock feature does not have to be set up to use the Attention Aware features.

After updating to iOS 27.3, the features should be automatically enabled. You can enable or disable the feature in Settings → Accessibility → Face Recognition & Attention. You can also enable Haptic on Successful Unlock there, just like an iPhone with Face ID.

In my experience, Attention Aware features will lower the volume of alarms, timers, and incoming calls when your iPhone is already unlocked. It also will prevent the display from dimming and locking while you are actively looking at it. Finally, it will expand and show notification content on the Lock Screen after unlocking with the new face unlock feature.

#3176. Max Hodak’s Science raises $400m to take its sight-restoring chip to the US

The Series D values the brain-computer interface company at $3.5bn, TechCrunch reports. Science will use it to expand PRIMA across Europe and to seek FDA approval in the US.

Science CEO Max Hodak on Centre Stage at Web Summit 2025 in Lisbon

Science Corporation, the brain-computer interface company founded by former Neuralink president Max Hodak, has raised a $400m Series D. The round values it at $3.5bn, a person familiar with the deal told TechCrunch.

Backers include Khosla Ventures, the Ackman Oxman Institute, Tenet Healthcare and Y Combinator, Science said in a blog post. It has now raised more than $900m since 2021.

Science’s first product, PRIMA, is a wearable and implantable chip for people with age-related macular degeneration. Science says it is the first brain-computer interface with a CE mark to restore “form vision”. That is the ability to read letters, numbers and words.

The round comes a few months after PRIMA’s launch in Europe, where it is available in Germany. Science will use the money to make PRIMA available across more of Europe and to prepare a US launch.

In the US, Science is seeking FDA approval through the Humanitarian Device Exemption, a route for rare conditions. It persuaded the FDA that advanced macular degeneration in both eyes is uncommon enough to qualify, TechCrunch reported. Science is also testing PRIMA in patients with Stargardt disease, another cause of blindness.

Science will also spend more on its biohybrid programme. It is a neural interface that joins engineered neurons to the brain’s own circuits. It is designing the first human trials with Yale neurosurgery professor Murat Günel, TechCrunch reported.

Hodak co-founded Neuralink in 2016 and was its president for four years before starting Science. The new money will also expand Science’s research, manufacturing and operations.

Other brain-interface startups have raised smaller rounds. Bridge Neurotech raised $13.5m in October for an ultrasound-based interface. In Europe, Barcelona’s INBRAIN Neuroelectronics is developing graphene brain implants.

AI data centers are using a shocking amount of electricity

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Every time you ask ChatGPT a question, generate an image with Gemini, or have Claude help write an email, a data center somewhere is doing the work. Most of us never think about what it takes to keep those servers running, but new research suggests America's AI infrastructure already has an enormous environmental cost.

A new Harvard-led study published in Nature Sustainability finds that 403 of the largest U.S. data centers consumed about 1.8% of the country's total electricity between May 2024 and April 2025.

That's an estimated 82 terawatt-hours of electricity in a single year, enough to power nearly 7 million American homes for a year, according to an Associated Press report.

And electricity consumption is only part of the problem. Researchers estimate the facilities produced 25.7 million metric tons of carbon dioxide emissions, roughly equivalent to Denmark's annual emissions.

Companies are racing to build more infrastructure to support increasingly powerful AI models, but questions remain over what the technology's rapid growth means for the environment and the people living near the facilities powering it.

Using satellite imagery, facility information and federal electricity-generation data, the team estimated how much power each location consumed and the resulting carbon emissions.

Approximately 54% of the electricity attributed to the data centers came from fossil-fuel generation, including 38% from natural gas and 15% from coal.

Sign up to the Tom's AI Guide weekly newsletter summing up all the biggest AI news you need to know. Plus, analysis from our AI editors and tips on how to use the latest AI tools!

The estimated emissions were also two to three times higher than an earlier assessment of hyperscale data-center emissions in 2018. The study's measurements ended in April 2025, which means they don't even account for the additional data centers built or expanded over the past year and a half.

As AI companies release more capable models and add features such as image generation, video creation and autonomous agents, demand for computing infrastructure continues to grow.

However, the study doesn't tell us exactly how much electricity one ChatGPT conversation consumes, or whether Gemini uses more power than Claude.

The researchers couldn't distinguish between electricity used for AI-specific workloads and traditional cloud-computing operations. That means the findings shouldn't be interpreted as emissions caused exclusively by generative AI.

Still, they provide a revealing look at the infrastructure supporting the AI services millions of people are adopting. And unlike the electricity consumed by a household appliance, the environmental impact of an AI request isn't necessarily visible to the person using the technology.

Power plants that burn fossil fuels release pollutants that can affect air quality and human health.

The Harvard researchers pointed to fine particulate matter, nitrogen oxides and sulfur dioxide as pollutants associated with fossil-fuel generation. Exposure to these pollutants is linked to respiratory and cardiovascular problems.

That means communities located near power plants could experience environmental consequences from data centers operating miles away.

The researchers did not directly measure those health effects, but they identified the issue as an important area for future investigation.

Location also makes a difference. The study found that Virginia, Oregon, Ohio, and Iowa accounted for more than half of the electricity consumption across the facilities examined.

Some data centers also operate in regions where electricity generation is substantially more carbon-intensive than the national average.

Using cleaner electricity, improving hardware efficiency and making data-center energy consumption more transparent could all help reduce the industry's environmental footprint.

But there's a fundamental challenge. As AI becomes faster, cheaper and more widely available, more people and businesses are finding reasons to use it.

For consumers, the takeaway is that AI may feel effortless, but the infrastructure behind it is anything but. And as the technology becomes part of everyday life, the question is how much energy we're willing to use to make it happen.

#3173. 28 Zero-Day Findings in Under Two Days. Is Robotics Security Keeping Pace?

VicOne’s AI-assisted research reveals what faster zero-day discovery means for robot safety

VicOne is a Physical AI cybersecurity company protecting vehicles and robots from cyber threats that can alter behavior and compromise safety.

VicOne used AI to find 28 zero-day vulnerabilities in Physical AI tools —these weaknesses can impact robot training, testing, and real-world control.

This article is brought to you by VicOne.

VicOne identified an initial set of 28 zero-day findings in less than two days using AI-assisted research across software and tools supporting the Physical AI ecosystem. These include projects developed or maintained by Google, NVIDIA, and Meta, among others.

Based on initial validation, all 28 findings are classified as zero-day vulnerabilities. The count may change following vendor and vulnerability-authority review, and some findings do not yet have CVE tracking numbers.

Many of these tools help teams train, simulate, test, and operate robots. Weaknesses in them could influence the models teams build, the test results they trust, and the instructions sent to robots.

These findings create two demands for robotics teams: responding as AI helps uncover weaknesses faster, and assessing how each one could affect robot safety and operations.

Vulnerability discovery involves examining code, tracing how systems communicate, and testing whether a suspected weakness can actually be exploited. AI can accelerate parts of this work, helping researchers analyze more software in less time. Attackers could use similar capabilities.

When the weakness is a zero-day — previously unknown and without an available fix — faster discovery can leave teams with little time to respond. While that exposure does not necessarily mean an attack has occurred, teams still need to determine whether they use the affected software and what an attacker could access or change.

VicOne’s findings span three stages of the robotics lifecycle: development and training, simulation and validation, and deployment and runtime. Weaknesses at each stage could affect what a robot learns, how it is tested, and how it is controlled.

Figure 1. In this research set, 75% of findings involved development, training, simulation, or validation tools, highlighting risks that can arise before a robot is deployed.VicOne

The following scenarios show how a compromised component could influence the robot at each stage.

These are potential consequences and not demonstrated outcomes for every finding. Actual effects depend on the attacker’s access, the system’s design, and whether other safeguards prevent the changes from reaching physical behavior.

In a separate demonstration, VicOne researchers provide a concrete example of a weakness affecting a protective function. The researchers exploited a vulnerability to prevent a robot’s remote-stop command from working. The case shows why teams need to test whether safeguards remain effective when the software supporting them is compromised.

Video 1. VicOne researchers demonstrate a vulnerability that prevents a robot’s remote-stop command from working. VicOne

AI can shorten the search for weaknesses, but a robotics team still needs to determine whether a fix is safe to deploy. Even after a software maintainer releases a patch, teams must identify affected systems, check compatibility, and verify that the update preserves intended behavior.

An earlier successful test remains useful evidence. However, a newly discovered weakness may reveal conditions that test never examined.

When immediate updating is impractical, teams may need temporary safeguards, such as restricting access to an affected service, while a validated fix is prepared.

As details from the 28 findings become available through coordinated disclosure, the next step is for robotics manufacturers is to connect each finding to its potential effect on development, deployment, and robot behavior.

That work also requires understanding how threats could affect robot behavior and how to protect systems already in operation. VicOne Radeis helps teams identify potential zero-day vulnerabilities, assess AI model and system security, and use simulation to evaluate how these risks could affect robot behavior before deployment. VicOne Rthena supports threat detection and responses within approved policies during operation.

Figure 2. Cybersecurity strengthens robot safety evidence throughout the lifecycle. VicOne helps teams test safety limits against manipulation before deployment and monitor the conditions behind safe behavior in operation.VicOne

Faster vulnerability discovery matters when teams can turn findings into action: identify what needs attention, verify that safeguards still hold, and confirm that a fix does not introduce new risks. That is how cybersecurity strengthens robot safety as systems continue to change.

#3171. Huffington and Rattner tell Semafor the tech industry has an image problem

Steven Rattner called the idea of Jensen Huang returning to Nvidia “ridiculous,” while Huffington said some tech leaders lack wisdom.

Arianna Huffington, now founder and chief executive of Thrive Global, pictured in 2011.

Arianna Huffington and Steven Rattner said on Monday that the tech industry is failing to win over a wary public. The two spoke on a panel at Semafor’s Silicon Valley & The World event, Semafor reported.

Huffington, who founded and runs behaviour-change company Thrive Global, called the Nvidia scandal a teachable moment. She said former Nvidia boss Jensen Huang had joined a group of “brilliantly intelligent” leaders who “just lack wisdom.”

“We need to invest in making humans better,” Huffington said, according to Semafor.

Huang quit as Nvidia’s chief executive last week. Since then, he has discussed a possible return, the Financial Times reported, and some in tech want him back.

Rattner, chief executive of Willett Advisors, called that idea “ridiculous.” He also rejected comparisons with OpenAI’s Sam Altman, who got his job back days after being ousted in 2023.

“You can’t bring Jensen back,” Rattner said.

Semafor, citing a CNBC report, said Nvidia’s board is not considering a return. TNW has not read the CNBC report directly.

Both speakers said tech leaders must do more to explain themselves to an anxious public. Rattner pointed to this month’s US midterm elections, which many saw as a rebuke of the industry.

“The crisis that the tech industry faces is the fact that people hate the tech industry and they hate AI,” Rattner said.

In those elections, voters rejected data centre plans in all but one of 41 ballot measures on the issue, Al Jazeera reported. Rattner said tech leaders, like politicians, have a duty to explain their work, and that the industry had failed to do so.

#3169. Advanced Metrology for Defect Detection, Tool Health, and Semiconductor Yield Enhancement



In advanced semiconductor manufacturing, small defects can have a large effect on yield. Thin film deposition tools must stay stable and qualified. Process drift must be caught early. When a defect does appear, engineers need to know where it came from and how it affects device performance. This webinar shows how in-line inspection and offline characterization combine into one workflow, from tool monitoring to root-cause analysis.

In the first half, Dr. Bitan Chakraborty from Intel, explains how surface scan metrology fits into station monitors for thin film tools. The session shows how baseline signatures and real-time monitoring reveal hardware wear, particle generation, and process drift before they reach production wafers. It then moves to in-line scans on patterned wafers. These scans expose layer-level defects and show how they form and spread through multi-layer device stacks. Linking this defect data to electrical test results helps teams find root causes and focus their yield improvement work.

In the second half, Dr. Jacob Petersen from Evident Scientific, addresses a common question: what happens after an in-line tool flags a problem? In-line tools are fast, but they cannot always provide the details needed for a firm conclusion. Offline 3D optical profilometry fills that gap by combining three complementary inspection techniques in a single system. It delivers dimensional measurements and helps determine whether a defect lies within the sample or comes from foreign material. The session covers how several optical techniques support inspection from bare silicon to fully packaged chips. It also shows how automation enables fast measurement of features down to the sub-nanometer scale with minimal operator handling.

What You Will Learn:

  • How surface scan metrology in station monitors tracks tool health and supports the qualification of thin film deposition processes
  • How baseline signatures and real-time monitoring detect particle generation, hardware degradation, and process drift before production is affected
  • How in-line scans on patterned wafers reveal layer-level defects and show how they propagate through multi-layer device structures
  • When offline 3D optical profilometry should follow in-line inspection, and how it measures dimensions and separates sample defects from foreign material
  • How correlating tool health data, inspection results, and electrical performance links physical defects to yield loss and guides targeted improvement projects

If there’s one upgrade I’m looking forward to seeing most on the iPhone 20 Pro, it’s the camera. The latest rumor has me excited because Apple is reportedly introducing a far more advanced imaging sensor, which could deliver dramatic improvements.

Although the iPhone 18 Pro Max is still one of the best camera phones around today, I was somewhat disappointed to find minimal upgrades in my iPhone 18 Pro Max vs. iPhone 17 Pro Max face-off. In almost every snapshot, the differences between them were nearly indistinguishable.

That’s why all eyes will be on Apple’s next flagship release. According to Weibo leaker Ice Universe, the iPhone 20 Pro could feature a main camera sensor with logic circuitry manufactured on a new 17-nanometer process. Even though this doesn’t directly mean the sensor itself will be physically larger, a more advanced logic layer gives the camera the capacity to deliver faster readout speeds, handle more complex image processing, and consume less power.

Here’s what I think that could mean in practice:

Most people don’t realize all the complex actions that go on behind the scenes the moment they tap the shutter button. The phone isn’t just capturing a single frame — it’s taking a rapid series of shots and processing them together to deliver one final image.

By introducing a more advanced image sensor that processes data faster, Apple could dramatically improve the iPhone 20 Pro’s dynamic range performance. Think about tricky, high-contrast lighting scenes where bright highlights compete with deep shadows. With a faster readout speed, the sensor could capture and merge exposures more effectively to balance those challenging areas.

Instead of leaving hotspots blown out by harsh light, the iPhone 20 Pro could better preserve detail in the highlights — all while lifting the shadows. You can see some of examples I'm referring to in the gallery above.

Sign up to the Tom's iGuide weekly newsletter with coverage on everything from product launches to software updates, this is your go-to source for the latest updates on all the best Apple content.

Apple has already made strides in this next area, but a more advanced image sensor could push things even further. I’m referring to zero shutter lag and reduced rolling shutter distortion when capturing fast-moving subjects. If you’ve ever tried photographing someone playing sports, you’re probably familiar with how easily those frames can come out blurry or out of focus.

Frenetic movement can make it tough to freeze a moment cleanly, so an image sensor with faster readout speeds would be much better equipped to handle the action. Just look at the side-by-side shots above of someone riding an electric scooter.

I shoot a ton of videos and know firsthand how quickly a phone can feel toasty whenever I record for more than a couple of minutes. If you really want to see how warm it gets, try shooting continuously for 10 minutes or longer.

Sustained capture like that demands serious processing power, which quickly leads to heat buildup. With a more power-efficient sensor, the iPhone 20 Pro could be better equipped to handle longer ProRes recording sessions without pausing due to overheating.

The iPhone 20 Pro is still a long way away, but this 17nm sensor rumor could become much more exciting if the sensor size itself increases. Apple certainly delighted us with a mechanical variable aperture main camera on the iPhone 18 Pro and 18 Pro Max, yet a physically larger sensor would be a compelling reason to upgrade to the iPhone 20 Pro.

This wouldn’t just improve its light-gathering abilities, but would also help boost detail, sharpness, and definition. If these leaks pan out, next year's anniversary iPhone could deliver the biggest leap in iPhone photography we've seen in years.
