For 33 years, Jensen Huang was Nvidia (NVDA -1.21%). Today after the market closes, the company reports its fiscal 2027 third-quarter results, followed by an earnings call led by Colette Kress, interim CEO and CFO.

The backward-looking figures still matter, but will only serve as a closing tally of the Huang era. The call will be Nvidia’s real post-founder stability test. Here’s what we’ll be watching out for:

Nvidia’s business is excellent, but the stock now carries three open questions: who leads, how revenue is reported, and what the investigation finds. Wait for answers before making your next move.

The Nasdaq fell 2.49% yesterday. The S&P 500 wasn’t far behind, slipping 1.92%.

Weeks like this tempt investors to do one of two things. Some sell a long-held winner (e.g. Nvidia) because the headlines look scary. Others rush into the hottest new name (like Anthropic). Either move can matter as much as which stocks you own.

That’s why the Rule Breakers approach begins with behavior. This week, two of the six habits deserve extra attention.

Picture two investors who bought Garmin (GRMN +0.12%) on March 17, 2022. That’s the day Team Rule Breakers recommended it in Stock Advisor, at $111.93. Within months, sales started slipping. The stock fell to the low $80s. It didn’t climb back above $111.93 until late 2023. The first investor gave up during the slump and sold. The second gave the business time. Today, the shares trade around $283. The second investor’s patience paid off.

Sitting through the slump was only half the job. By late 2024, Garmin had roughly doubled from its recommendation price. That’s when many investors sell half to “play with the house’s money.” Anyone who cashed out at the double, around $224, have missed about another 25% since. Big winners rarely rise in a straight line. Letting one run means sitting through the swings.

You can’t control how Nvidia’s report lands or how Anthropic’s shares trade on day one. But you can choose how you respond.

Nvidia itself shows why that matters. It has been a standout pick for both Team Rule Breakers and Team Hidden Gems over the years. Hidden Gems’ May 2024 recommendation is still about 25 percentage points ahead of the S&P 500, despite the recent slide. Investors who let it run have been well rewarded.

Every Garmin investor in this story owned a good pick, too. Their results came down to what they did next.

The holiday shopping season starts with a checkup, with three consumer favorites reporting before the market opens on Wednesday.

Team Rule Breakers sees CrowdStrike (CRWD -3.04%) reaching $365 within five years, an implied annualized return of around 10%. It has been recommended three times in Rule Breakers, and all three are beating the S&P 500 by triple digits. As hackers become more sophisticated and digital break-ins more costly, businesses need cyber protection more than ever.

Our thesis for CrowdStrike held that “cybersecurity is essential for any business on the cloud, and that has become even more mission-critical these days.” That statement holds up remarkably well. The company’s AI-powered Falcon threat intelligence platform works to detect and prevent breaches before they start.

Given the prevalence of AI-powered threats, the company’s strong industry position, and continued impressive growth, we believe there’s a long runway of growth ahead for CrowdStrike.

#3107. If the November Windows update fails to install on your PC, here’s what to do

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Tech > Services & Software > Operating Systems > Windows > Windows 11

This month’s security update is failing on some systems already running the preview update released in October. But there is a fix afoot.

Ah, Microsoft. Another Windows update, another glitch. This latest one affects some Windows 11 users who attempt to install this week’s November Patch Tuesday update, only for it to fail. But don’t worry, there’s already a fix in play.

Also: You can now restore Windows 11 even if it can’t boot up – here’s how

On its support page to the November update designated KB5132061, Microsoft revealed and explained this latest problem.

Windows users who installed the November preview update released on October 28 may run into a glitch when trying to install the actual November update released on November 10. In this case, the installation may fail to complete. Your PC might repeatedly try to install the update or you may simply see an error code such as 0x80070306, 0x800f0989, or 0x800f0993.

I can confirm the problem. I installed the preview update on one of my Windows 11 virtual machines. Trying to then install the actual November update triggered the installation error.

If you’re in the same boat, what can you do to fix this dilemma? Just be patient.

Also: Windows finally gets a built-in internet speed test tool – how to try it

Microsoft promises that all affected PCs should receive repairs within 24 to 48 hours starting from November 11, 1pm ET. For this, make sure your PC is connected to the internet and is set up to receive updates via Windows Update. Head to Settings and select Windows Update. You may already find the November update known as 2026-11 Security Update (KB5132061) (26300.9974) available again. If so, select it to install it, and the process should work now.

I tried this on my virtual machine, and the November update installed without a hitch. But if you still bump into errors, check out Microsoft’s support page on troubleshooting problems updating Windows.

Microsoft typically releases each monthly Windows update in two phases.

First, there’s an optional preview update that kicks off around the end of the previous month. This one is considered a non-security update because it contains only feature changes. In this case, the preview update for November was released on October 28. Labeled KB5127936, this one unveiled the new customizable right-click menu, Cloud rebuild option, and other feature changes.

Also: You can change Windows settings directly from a search now

Second, there’s the actual mandatory Patch Tuesday update that contains both security patches and the non-security changes. Here, the November KB5132061 update was rolled out on November 10.

The preview updates are designed for IT administrators, software testers, and others who want an early look. That means they aren’t always fully baked and may contain a few bugs. But since they pop up in Windows Update, anyone can install them.

The actual Patch Tuesday updates are for all Windows users. In this case, there seemed to be an incompatibility or other conflict between the two updates that Microsoft then had to resolve.

#3106. I spent 4 weeks testing a $319 headband designed to beat insomnia but slept better the night I stopped using it — here's what happened

Join the Tom's Guide Club for quick access. Enter your email below and we'll send confirmation, and sign you up to our newsletter.

The Spatial Sleep Headband uses audio resonance therapy to improve your sleep but it's an uphill climb to get there. Vibrating your skull while filling your brain with unusual noises, the first few nights are rough going, but it does eventually pay off... slightly. The soothing noises became a pleasant bedtime addition but any sleep changes were minimal. At $319, it's a heavy investment in tech that takes a while to show results.

Clinical research suggests it can help insomnia

First few weeks are disruptive to your sleep

Why you can trust Tom's Guide Our writers and editors spend hours analyzing and reviewing products, services, and apps to help find what's best for you. Find out more about how we test, analyze, and rate.

When you can't sleep, you'll try anything to drift off. But I can almost guarantee you've never tried something like the Spatial Sleep Headband. This peculiar wearable uses acoustic resonance to send you snoozing. I put it to the test and yes, it's as weird as it sounds.

Type: Sleep headbandBest for: Insomnia, trouble falling asleepDimensions: 4" x 7.8" x 3.7"Weight: 2.5 ozWarranty: 90 days limitedPrice: $319 at SoundHealth

The Spatial Sleep Band sits on your forehead where it vibrates and plays sound. With regular use this combo should train your brain's neural response to build better sleep, no hard work required. Although I'll be honest, the Spatial Sleep Band isn't what I'd describe as easy.

I used the Spatial Sleep headband nightly for four weeks and I'll dive into my full experience below. In brief, it's an odd sensation and one that comes with a steep learning curve. And while eventually the Spatial Sleep Band does become a soothing addition to your bedtime routine, it's a struggle to get to that point.

As someone with only mild sleep issues, I've yet to see any real benefit from the Spatial Sleep Band. And the adjustment period was frustrating enough that I'd have given up if it wasn't my job to keep going. For those with more severe sleep problems, the annoyance of the Spatial Sleep Headband will likely feel like less of an intrusion, and the benefits more noticeable.

But it's an expensive gamble, with a Spatial Sleep Headband costing $319 (although that's slightly more affordable than similar sleep headbands like the Muse S Athena and the Elemind). You do get a 45-day return period as well, and by that point you should have a good idea if this product is for you. And it's subscription-free — that's rare for this kind of sleep tech.

The Spatial Sleep Headband costs $319 — an investment, for sure, but this is a fairly standard price tag for a high-tech sleep aid. There's no subscription required and a 45-day returns policy is included.

The overall design of the Spatial Sleep Headband is relatively simple. The slim band is made from a soft material and the Velcro strap is easy to adjust.

Its secret lies on the inside, where you'll find two purple nodules. These press against the forehead and deliver the acoustic vibration that makes the Spatial Headband work.

Get instant access to breaking news, the hottest reviews, great deals and helpful tips.

There's one more important part to the Spatial and that's the three lines on the front of the design. These are used to align the band with the center of your face, to ensure the sound is delivered to the right part of the forehead.

I used the Spatial Sleep Headband for four weeks as part of my usual routine, wearing it to bed (with an eye mask). Here's how I rate the performance...

Setting up the Spatial Sleep Headband is simple, for a piece of complex tech. First you have to charge it, then turn the headband on (there's a button on the front) and connect it to the app.

You'll be asked to scan your face — this helps Spatial create a sound just right for you. When you're ready to sleep, get the band in position and press start on the app.

The sound automatically plays for 45 minutes, at which point you should be asleep (fingers crossed). You can pause and restart the sound from the app, in case of late night wake ups.

The battery lasts for roughly 90 minutes, or two sessions, and I have used mine through two nights without charging. However, I recommend charging after every session, to avoid the sound cutting out. A USB-C cable is provided and charging takes roughly 30 minutes.

The app is mostly used to kick off the audio at night, but there's a fun memory game you can play as well.

I'm normally game for testing any kind of weird sleep tech but when I first strapped the Spatial Band to my head, I felt like I'd made a terrible mistake. Nodules pressed into my forehead and my bones rattled to a dissonant hum that sounded like pans clattering to the ground in the distance. I clenched my jaw and waited for it to end.

There was an important lesson here, echoed in the bright red dents on my forehead: do not over-tighten the band.

With a slightly looser band, night two went better. But the first week was rough. The sound and sensations of the Spatial Headband are far removed from my usual sleep comforts. I was hoping using it would help me drift off quickly but instead I lay awake, questioning the life choices that had led me to this moment.

Spatial does warn that it takes persistence before you see results and week two went better. The sound and I had gotten used to each other, meaning it no longer sat at the forefront of my mind. Now I enjoyed a pleasant background hum and only occasionally worried about my vibrating skull.

By week three I could see a glimmer of progress. The distant drone of the sleep headband had grown relaxing. One night, on the brink of sleep, I even found myself wondering what the pleasant noise was.

These benefits have yet to be reflected in my sleep score, however. On some nights it still takes me up upwards of 30 minutes to drift off fully. And I'm still experiencing brief wake ups in the night. (Including waking up to take the headband off — the nodules are uncomfortable when they press against your face.)

Last night, having reached the end of my four weeks testing period, I decided to ditch the headband and go back to my usual sleep patterns. I got an 88 sleep score from my Oura Ring, my highest in 12 nights.

As someone with only minor sleep problems, the Spatial Sleep Headband is a steep learning curve for a small advantage. But I don't want to write it off entirely. There are strong reviews from other users and Spatial has conducted some notable research. Spatial is designed to improve your natural sleep frequency, so for those who have a sleep routine that's completely off-beat, the Spatial sleep might help set the pace you need.

The Spatial Headband uses acoustic vibrations and sleep-friendly frequencies to improve the quality and quantity of your sleep. It requires regular use to see the results and after several weeks the strange hum of the Spatial should be the backdrop to a decent night's rest.

The problem is that those first weeks are challenging, to put it mildly. From the sound to the feel, the Spatial band is simply strange to use. It feels like a disruptive force and you might be tempted to give up before you feel the benefits. Or rather, if you feel the benefits — I stuck with mine and noticed only minor differences.

✅ You're experiencing long-term sleep deprivation: The Spatial Sleep Headband didn't work for me but it is backed by some serious research. Its impact might be more noticeable when overcoming bigger sleep problems.

✅ You've tried all kinds of sleep tech and nothing works: Acoustic resonance is unusual and not the kind of sleep enhancer you pick up on a whim. If you're struggling to improve your sleep, this might be worth a try.

✅ You're kept awake by disruptive noise: When the Spatial band is on, it drowns out most other sounds. That's good news if traffic or rowdy neighbors are contributing to your sleep problems.

❌ You want a quick solution: Spatial suggests it takes three to four weeks to feel the benefit of the Sleep Headband, and I found week one to be a steep learning curve. The Muse S Athena sleep headband was much easier to get used to.

❌ You share a bed with a light sleeper: Some sound does leak from the Spatial headband which might disturb co-sleepers.

❌ You want a small sleep boost, rather than a total overhaul: For minor sleep issues the Spatial Sleep Band is a pricey investment that takes time to get used to. Try low-cost options like sleepy tea and guided meditations before diving in with the Spatial.

The Muse S Athena uses your brainwaves to track your sleep and, when it senses you're about to be disturbed, plays a sleep-inducing sound to send you back under. I tested it and found the performance impressive but it is a premium buy, retailing for $479.99 at Muse and Amazon.

The Snoozeband isn't as high-tech as the other options listed here but this comfortable set of sleep headphones can help you drift off in noisy environments. It utilizes thin speakers in a soft headband to deliver sleep sounds without the discomfort of an earbud. From $49.99 at Snoozeband.

#3105. Your Microwave Can Poach an Egg Better Than You’d Expect

I used to save poached eggs for lazy weekends. This microwave method made them part of my weekday routine.

My weekday breakfasts used to come down to a protein smoothie or scrambled eggs, mostly because both are fast.

Poached eggs, my favorite version, stayed on the weekend list because the stovetop method takes more babysitting than I can manage before work. A microwave was the key to changing all that.

Now, with just a small bowl of cold water and about a minute of cooking, I get a poached egg with a firm white and a soft yolk, ready to slide onto toast or greens. And it’s the best prep method I’ve found thus far.

This method demands just one minute, one bowl and leaves no mess, save for the quick rinse of a wet mug. The results are surprisingly good and the process is impossible to flub. You can easily tinker with timing to get the exact consistency you’re after.

So ditch the frying pan or sluggish pot of boiling water. Here’s how to make perfect poached eggs in under 60 seconds.

Read more: Achieve Your Daily Protein Goals With This Simple Visual Guide

Step 1: Fill a ramekin with a half-cup of salted, room-temperature water. It must be enough to submerge the egg.

You’ll want enough water to submerge the egg but not spill over the top of the ramekin.

Step 2: Crack one egg and carefully drop it into the water, trying not to disturb its structural integrity.

Step 3: Place the ramekin in the microwave and cook on high for about 45 seconds, longer if you prefer a firmer yolk.

Cook the submerged egg for 40 seconds for a runny yolk and closer to a minute for a firm one.

Step 4: Remove the egg gently from the water with a slotted spoon or wire skimmer.

Lift your egg carefully out of the water with a slotted spoon or mesh strainer.

Step 5: Serve over toast or a bed of greens with avocado, hot sauce, chili crisp and other accompaniments.

In one or two tries you’ll be able to fine-tune your poached egg to your perfect doneness and then nail it every time.

Note: The base temperature for any microwave will vary, and thus, cook times may also. Try 40 to 45 seconds for your first effort, then add five-second increments for subsequent tries until you achieve the desired doneness.

I haven’t experienced any egg-related explosions, but a Reddit deep dive into microwave egg poachers unearthed a nugget of advice: Avoid yolk explosions by poking it through with a toothpick.

Stick that fluffy puff of protein on a piece of toast with some spinach, top it all with flaky salt, hot sauce or hollandaise and have a cafe-quality breakfast in less time than it takes to brew coffee. You can also use them to top a salad or serve over rice with pickled vegetables and chili crisp for a light lunch.

Cooking bacon in the oven is the cleanest method and results in even crispier strips, with no greasy stovetop to clean afterward. A fast water boil with these two pantry ingredients lifts stubborn stains from your best cookware without all the manic scrubbing. Here are nine more cooking hacks that save time, energy, and money.

If you don’t want to cook, this is my favorite prepared meal delivery service for 2025.

A small batch of bacon cooked in the air fryer can be another quick protein value add to your breakfast in the morning and it’s a perfect pairing with your microwave-poached egg.

You can prevent your egg yolk from exploding by starting with a small increment of time in the microwave, like 45 seconds. If you need to heat the egg more, you can add increments of five seconds as needed. Poking the egg yolk with a toothpick before putting the egg in the microwave may also help prevent an explosion during or after poaching the egg.

Using your microwave to poach eggs is a quick way to get some protein added to your breakfast or lunch, and it’s a completely safe way to cook the egg as long as you add small increments to the microwave timer.

#3104. Why a Data Center Slowdown Would Reach Utilities and Electrical Suppliers Before Chipmakers

If the data center build-out starts to hit delays and speed bumps, it will affect the various industries involved differently.

Voters across the United States supported restrictions on data center development or rejected proposals favoring new projects in 40 of 41 local ballot contests on Nov. 3, according to Ballotpedia. The results included five full construction bans and three six-month moratoriums, raising the likelihood that some planned data centers will be delayed or canceled.

A slowdown in construction could reduce future infrastructure spending by electric utilities and cut into orders for electrical equipment.

However, chipmaker Nvidia (NVDA -1.21%) could continue selling chips to existing data centers and new projects in other locations. Hence, the earliest signs of a slowdown in the build-out may appear in electricity contracts and equipment orders rather than chip sales.

Data center developers often request electricity capacity from utilities while their projects are still in the planning stages. However, not all of these requests lead to actual construction.

Developers initially requested more than 30,000 megawatts of electricity capacity from American Electric Power's (AEP -0.37%) Ohio subsidiary. After American Electric Power Ohio introduced requirements for paid engineering studies and binding financial commitments, requests totaling 13,023 megawatts proceeded to studies. Developers had signed new contracts for only 5,642 megawatts by February 2026. Another 12,219 megawatts had already been contracted before American Electric Power Ohio's new data center tariff took effect in July 2025.

This does not mean actual electricity demand declined. Instead, many developers that initially requested power capacity did not proceed with binding contracts. A similar reduction in new commitments could signal slower future construction without immediately affecting electricity sales to existing customers.

Growing electricity demand from data centers can create new investment opportunities for utilities. Large projects may require new power plants, substations, and transmission lines, allowing regulated utilities to earn returns on additional infrastructure investments.

This opportunity is reflected in American Electric Power's expansion plans. The company expects 84 gigawatts of incremental contracted load by 2031. To support that growing demand, the company plans to invest about $100 billion from 2027 through 2031, primarily in power generation, transmission, and distribution. These investments are expected to increase its rate base, or the value of regulated assets on which it can earn returns, to $162 billion by 2031.

However, if some of those planned data centers are delayed or canceled, American Electric Power may need to postpone some of its own infrastructure investments. This could slow its earnings growth, although lower capital spending would also reduce its borrowing needs. Hence, a reduction in new data center projects would affect utilities' future growth opportunities before reducing their current electricity sales.

Data center construction also drives demand for transformers, switchgear, and other electrical equipment. If new projects are delayed, suppliers could receive fewer orders while continuing to deliver equipment already booked.

Eaton (ETN +0.39%) manufactures electrical equipment used in data centers and other industries. In the third quarter, it reported that orders from data center customers across its electrical businesses more than doubled over the preceding 12 months.

Eaton ended the third quarter with $26.2 billion in firm orders awaiting delivery. About 72% of these orders are targeted for delivery within the next 12 months. The backlog includes orders from industries other than data centers.

Hence, a slowdown in new orders might not immediately affect Eaton's revenue. However, if orders continue weakening, the company could eventually face slower sales growth and lower factory utilization.

At its Nov. 12 closing price, Eaton traded at about 26 times its expected 2026 adjusted earnings. Slower earnings growth could put pressure on this valuation. However, demand from utilities, industrial customers, and aerospace could help offset weakness in its data center business.

Chipmakers may not face the same immediate impact from delayed data center construction. Their customer will likely continue to buy chips to upgrade existing facilities or install them at other locations with available electricity and cooling capacity.

Nvidia is scheduled to report its fiscal third-quarter results on Nov. 17. The company was guiding for total revenue of $108 billion, plus or minus 2%, up from $96.2 billion in the second quarter. However, its actual results will provide a more recent indicator of demand for its artificial intelligence (AI) chips.

Microsoft (MSFT -1.65%) has already demonstrated how chip spending could remain strong despite data center construction delays. In its recently reported quarter, Microsoft's capital expenditures totaled $45.2 billion. Approximately three-quarters of this spending was for shorter-lived assets such as CPUs, GPUs, memory, and storage. This spending continued despite delays in third-party data center capacity.

However, prolonged construction delays could eventually affect chip demand, as new servers require sufficient power and cooling capacity. Nvidia had $279 billion in supply and manufacturing capacity commitments at the end of July, although some agreements can be adjusted before becoming firm orders. If customers delay chip purchases due to limited data center capacity, Nvidia could face risks associated with these commitments.

Hence, Nvidia's upcoming results and management's outlook could help investors assess whether data center construction delays are beginning to affect semiconductor demand.

#3102. iPhone Duo Gets a Facial Unlock Feature, but It’s Not Face ID. What to Know

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Our expert, award-winning staff selects the products we cover and rigorously researches and tests our top picks. If you buy through our links, we may earn a commission.

Unlocking Apple's foldable should get a lot easier, but there are some caveats.

One of the iPhone Duo‘s biggest drawbacks has just been addressed – mostly.

Unlike Apple’s other current iPhones, the iPhone Duo lacks Face ID, meaning you have to rely on the noticeably less speedy Touch ID or enter a passcode to unlock the foldable device. This would be less painful if the Duo didn’t cost $1,999, and if Face ID hadn’t long been a standard feature across the company’s other iPhones, including its most affordable option.

Now, there’s something of a fix. In its latest iOS 27.3 developer beta, Apple has added an option to unlock the iPhone Duo using the front camera. This should make accessing the phone’s contents more seamless and intuitive.

Until now, my least favorite aspect of using the iPhone Duo has been the inability to unlock using facial recognition – a limitation that stands in stark contrast to the foldable phone’s premium feel. Scanning a fingerprint with Touch ID not only feels antiquated for such a pricey device, but also rather slow. Samsung’s Galaxy Z Fold 8, by contrast, has a facial recognition feature, as well as fingerprint unlocking that’s much faster than the Duo’s.

It appears Apple heard our cries and is bringing a workaround to the Duo. This new unlocking capability isn’t quite the same as Face ID, a more secure biometric facial recognition and authentication system. Instead, the iPhone Duo will now let you unlock the phone using the selfie camera under slightly more limited conditions to help ensure security.

Read more: Meet the Custom-Built Machine That Has Folded the iPhone Duo 500,000 Times

To enable the new optional unlock feature, go to your Duo’s Settings and toggle it on under Touch ID & Passcode. Because unlocking with the Duo’s front camera isn’t as secure as using Touch ID or Face ID, you’ll need to use Touch ID or enter a passcode after around 45 minutes of inactivity. Touch ID is also required when using Apple Pay or accessing your passwords.

Unlocking with the front camera is possible because of a new capability in Apple silicon called Secure Exclaves. The iPhone Duo uses this to securely and privately process data of a user’s face and verify the match. That means iOS, apps, users and Apple can’t access the data used to unlock the phone via the front camera.

I admittedly didn’t think this update would arrive on Apple’s first-generation foldable; I assumed we’d just have to cross our fingers and hope for Face ID to land on the next iteration. It’s a relatively small improvement, but one that I think will make the Duo experience a lot more convenient and in line with the phone’s modern design and aesthetics, even if it’s not a full Face ID fix. As much as I thought I could make do with Touch ID, it turned out to be more of a nuisance than I’d anticipated; I’m so used to the speediness of unlocking by simply looking at a phone’s screen and swiping up. So I’m glad there’s a software update to help address that gap on the Duo.

The next iOS 27.3 developer beta also adds the option for the iPhone Duo to automatically lock when someone closes the phone. You can enable this under Settings > Display & Brightness.

Alongside other recent software updates, including the addition of Reachability to make the Duo’s cover screen content easier to access one-handed, and support for Apple Pencil with USB-C, Apple appears poised to continue rolling out features that make the Duo more adaptable.

#3100. Google’s Pixel Tag tracker won’t work as well on older Android phones – check our list

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Tech > Services & Software > Operating Systems > Mobile OS > Android

Several of the tracker’s best features require Bluetooth 6.0-compatible device.

Google’s Pixel Tag, the company’s take on an Android-exclusive Bluetooth tracker, is finally here, following its August announcement during the Google I/O developer conference.

Also: Google’s new Android XR glasses have lower ‘creep factor’ than competitors

Pixel Tag is a complete Bluetooth tracker for Android users that appears less confined to device-specific ecosystems than Samsung’s Smart Tag 3 and Apple’s AirTag.

However, if you look at Google’s footnotes, the Pixel Tag’s functionality is diminished when an older Android phone is involved. Several of the tracker’s best features require a compatible device running Android 9.0+ and Bluetooth 6.0+, according to Google.

Android 9 and newer encompasses a lot of devices, but Bluetooth 6.0 and newer doesn’t. Here’s what to check before you buy.

Smartphones began shipping with Bluetooth 6.0 in 2025, starting with the Samsung Galaxy S26 Plus and Galaxy S26 Ultra. The following phones also have Bluetooth 6.0:

If your Android phone is older than any of the listed above, even by a generation, it likely supports Bluetooth 5.3 or 5.4 — not enough for the Pixel Tag’s best features.

The Pixel Tag’s precision-finding capabilities are powered by Bluetooth Channel Sounding, a key feature introduced in Bluetooth 6.0. Nearly every review I’ve seen of the Pixel Tag, including our own, tests the tracker when paired with a Pixel 10, Pixel 10 Pro, Pixel 11, or Pixel 11 Pro.

I assume that Android users whose phones run Android 9.0+ but lack Bluetooth 6.0+ can use the Pixel Tag for very basic, general location tracking. These users may see the tracker’s general location, but Google’s device compatibility footnote appears several times throughout its press release.

The following features require Android 9.0+ and Bluetooth 6.0+, according to Google’s release:

So, on older Android devices without Android 9.0+ and Bluetooth 6.0+, the following aren’t supported: locating the exact direction and distance of your tracked devices, pinging a tracker when you don’t see it, or giving your tracked devices a custom name.

Also: 3 ways Bluetooth 7 upgrades your devices beyond lossless audio

Additionally, shorter-distance tracking requires an ultra-wideband chip inside your Android phone. Channel Sounding handles distance and direction at longer ranges, while UWB takes over for shorter ranges. Most premium Android phones with Bluetooth 6.0 also have UWB chips, but several of Google’s base-model phones lack a UWB chip.

Samsung’s base-model, A-series, and Z Flip-series phones also lack UWB, resulting in more phones that can’t access the Pixel Tag’s short-range precision finding capabilities.

With all the specs in mind, the Pixel Tag is the best option for users of recent premium flagship Android phones. Those without the latest Bluetooth connectivity will find that the Pixel Tag works like any other Bluetooth tracker, with basic functionality.

Also: These are the closest things to AirTags for Android users

The good thing is that a single Pixel Tag is $30, so it’s not much more expensive than a Tile Tag, and cheaper than a Chipolo Loop. Still, if your phone doesn’t support Bluetooth 6.0, you might be better off looking for a cheaper option until you’re ready to upgrade.

#3099. John Mulaney’s SNL Sister Eldercare Ad Is an Instant, Painful Classic

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Our expert, award-winning staff selects the products we cover and rigorously researches and tests our top picks. If you buy through our links, we may earn a commission.

How long did it take you to text it to your sibling group chat?

Did SNL just add another legendary fake commercial to the show’s hall of fame? On Saturday night, host John Mulaney and the cast delivered a winning pretaped parody commercial that hit a nerve in more than a few households.

In the ad, Mulaney and others fret about their aging parents. Nursing homes don’t appeal, yet in-home care would cost too much. Fortunately, Mulaney has heard about Sister, “a live-in, 24/7 eldercare provider that is completely free, and also your sister.”

“I love my mom more than anything,” says another adult son, played by Andrew Dismukes. “That doesn’t mean I want to help her in the bathroom. Sister doesn’t either. But she will, whereas I won’t. That’s the Sister difference!”

Jane Wickline plays a frantic sister who drops everything, quits her job, breaks her lease, and moves halfway across the country to take care of her elderly dad (Tommy Brennan, ironically one of the youngest cast members).

Mulaney says he just had to text his sister, “Dad fell,” and voilà, she instantly appeared.

Mikey Day plays a doctor who, as the author of the astutely named book Not It! A Son’s Guide to Elder Care, explains how it works.

“Years of internalized sexism warps Sister’s brain into thinking caretaking is her responsibility, and somehow, not yours,” Day says. “Next, your text arrives, instantly activating her. And that’s it! You’re done for life! See you at the funeral!”

Anyone who’s ever had to care for elderly parents can relate to Sister’s duties: Making those torturous, endless calls to doctors, insurance companies and pharmacists, all while screaming, “Speak to human!” at unhelpful phone trees.

Meanwhile, Kenan Thompson rejoices that he’s still in the will despite doing nothing, and Mulaney and Brennan bond over griping about Sister’s diet restrictions. Mulaney urges viewers to sign up now for the free addition of Sister’s Husband, who just doesn’t know why this burden has to fall on his (defensive) wife.

A quickly flashed line at the end of the ad notes, “Offer void if Sister has a good therapist,” who’d presumably tell her to insist her brothers do their share.

It wasn’t just a fictional sketch to some SNL viewers on Reddit.

“This isn’t funny, this is life for a lot of women,” wrote one person.

“I watched this skit earlier today with my husband, and I started crying,” said another. “It’s exactly the situation I’m in while my brother travels the world.”

The point of the ad is that the duties fell on one very human family member. But tech companies are increasingly eyeing that responsibility as an opportunity for AI or robotic help — if that’s something you and your family are willing to try.

One device we’ve seen is a companion robot, ElliQ, that’s meant to live with elderly family members and serve as a digital assistant, social companion and health advocate. (We tried it out with some of our parents and grandparents.) And a 2025 University of Michigan survey found that older adults often find AI smart home devices and voice assistants useful in helping them age in place. CNET also has a roundup of the most reliable smart tech to help people age in place.

No robot or AI can replace the personal touch and self-sacrificial dedication of Sister. I haven’t replayed an SNL parody commercial this many times since the now-classic 2017 ad for Alexa Echo Silver: For the Greatest Generation.

And yes, I texted the Sister ad to my two sisters (but not my brothers).

#3098. Forget Nvidia Stock at $160 per Share. Buy This Semiconductor ETF Instead.

Nvidia’s business is booming, but its headlines aren’t. Here’s a way to stay invested in AI chips without leaning on one company.

A month ago, Nvidia (NVDA -1.29%) was riding high as the dominant supplier of artificial intelligence (AI) chips. But wow, can things change fast in the stock market.

First, there was a sell-off in tech stocks, brought about by fears that spending was getting out of hand. Then the results of the midterm elections were seen to throw up roadblocks for data center approvals and construction. And finally, a scandal forced Nvidia founder Jensen Huang to resign, and investigators and Congress are probing the company's connections with a purported Chinese spy.

Now Nvidia is trading near $160, down 26% in the past month and 32% below its all-time high.

But there's an interesting disconnect here. Nvidia's business hasn't suddenly fallen apart. In fact, the company reported $96.2 billion in revenue in its fiscal 2027 second quarter, a whopping 106% increase from a year earlier. And big tech companies are expected to spend $800 billion on AI infrastructure this year, and more than $1 trillion next year.

Undoubtedly, there are plenty of opportunities in AI stocks. But if you want to limit your exposure to Nvidia and its bad headlines right now, a viable option is the VanEck Semiconductor ETF (SMH -0.34%). It might be the smartest investment you can make right now.

The VanEck Semiconductor ETF tracks the performance of the MVIS US Listed Semiconductor 25 index, which holds the largest and most liquid companies involved in chip production and equipment businesses that are listed on U.S. exchanges. Nvidia is the largest holding, at a little more than 17%. But the ETF also has several other companies at the forefront of AI-capable semiconductors -- including Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing, Broadcom, and Advanced Micro Devices. These three companies collectively make up nearly 23% of SMH, which has 26 holdings total.

Data source: VanEck, YCharts (performance as of Nov. 13, 2026).

The most notable fact from the table above? Nvidia is the only member of SMH's top holdings that is in the red so far in 2026. And while Nvidia is down more than 12% for the year, SMH shows a 35% gain.

The ETF charges a reasonable 0.35% annual expense ratio, or $35 annually per $10,000 invested. And you get exposure to AI processors, memory, chipmaking equipment, and other semiconductor businesses.

The semiconductor industry has more going for it than one company, regardless of how dominant Nvidia has become. For investors who want to stay invested in AI without making a $160 bet on Nvidia's next chapter, SMH looks like the more attractive choice.

#3097. Google Wallet just turned your Android phone into a digital house key – how it works

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Home & Office > Smart Home > Home Security

Google is moving digital keys out of individual smart lock apps and into the Google Wallet.

Google is adding digital home keys to Google Wallet, letting users tap their phones to unlock compatible smart locks. The home key functionality, which will integrate with Google Home, will roll out this month.

Also: This tiny box gives your older tech smart home superpowers

Apple introduced Home Keys in 2021 with iOS 15, allowing users to store digital keys in the Apple Wallet. This lets you tap your iPhone or Apple Watch on the lock to unlock it. More recently, the addition of Express Mode to Apple Home lets users unlock smart locks without first unlocking their iPhones with Face ID.

Google’s digital keys use tap-to-unlock via NFC on smart locks. Like the Apple Home Key, you don’t need to unlock your phone to use your digital key, though you can change your verification settings as you wish.

Google’s announcement confirms that the company is embracing Aliro and UWB unlocking technologies as well. UWB unlocking for smart locks is supported on Google Pixel 10 Pro and newer models, as well as select UWB-enabled Samsung Galaxy phones. Aliro is a common standard for compatible smart locks and devices.

Before Google’s announcement, compatible smart locks could be controlled on Android through their accompanying app and Google Home. Smart lock companies also offered their own digital access methods, like NFC cards, Bluetooth, and geolocation.

One digital key will be created for each Google Home, so it can unlock all compatible smart locks in that home. You won’t need to search through digital keys in Google Wallet to find the one for your front door, back door, or bedroom door — just tap your phone and Google Home will recognize the lock as one in your smart home ecosystem.

At launch, Google Wallet will support digital keys for the Aqara U400 with UWB and NFC, and NFC on the Schlage Sense Pro and Nuki Keypad 2.

Google Wallet already supports digital car keys for compatible vehicles.

#3096. Top Wall Street analysts suggest these 3 dividend stocks for consistent income

Inflation data, earnings reports and tensions in the Middle East have been influencing the market. In this volatile backdrop, investors seeking income can bolster their portfolios by adding dividend-paying stocks.

The recommendations of top Wall Street analysts can help inform investors in their search for attractive stocks from the vast universe of dividend-paying companies. These experts assign ratings after analyzing a company's financials and ability to consistently pay dividends while also seeking capital appreciation.

Here are three dividend-paying stocks that are highlighted by Wall Street's top pros, as tracked by TipRanks, a platform that ranks analysts based on their past performance.

Integrated oil and gas giant Exxon Mobil has increased its dividends for 43 consecutive years. At a quarterly dividend of $1.03 per share (annualized dividend of $4.12), XOM stock offers a yield of 2.6%.

In his latest research report on energy players, Morgan Stanley analyst Devin McDermott reiterated a buy rating on Exxon Mobil stock and increased his price target to $177 from $168.

The analyst raised his free cash flow estimates to reflect Q2 guidance and the oil price strip, with the largest increase noted for integrated players due to higher refining margins. Notably, the five-star analyst raised his cash flow estimates by an average of 20% for the second half of 2026 and 7% for 2027.

McDermott highlighted that while pure-play refiners have rallied on stronger margins, integrated energy stocks have lagged, creating relative-value opportunities in major North American integrated producers, including Exxon Mobil, Suncor and Cenovus Energy.

Overall, McDermott is bullish on Exxon Mobil, as he expects the company to deliver strong earnings and cash flow growth, driven by robust upstream volumes, high-value projects in Product Solutions, and more than $5 billion of additional structural cost savings.

"XOM's large global integrated operations and strong balance sheet (0.0x 2027 net leverage) make it a clear defensive play in an uncertain macro backdrop," said McDermott.

McDermott ranks No. 726 among more than 12,490 analysts tracked by TipRanks. His ratings have been profitable 59% of the time, delivering an average return of 9.80%. See Exxon Mobil Stock Buybacks on TipRanks.

Moving on to natural gas producer Expand Energy. The company announced a quarterly base dividend of $0.575 per share to be paid on Sept. 3. At an annualized dividend of $2.30 per share, EXE offers a yield of about 2.3%.

Recently, Goldman Sachs analyst Neil Mehta reaffirmed a buy rating on Expand Energy stock and increased his price target to $113 from $99. Mehta attributed his higher price target to cash flow improvement and a strong outlook for shareholder returns. He also cited the stock's attractive valuation, with an 11% free cash flow, or FCF, yield based on his 2027/2028 estimates compared with the peer average of 9%.

The five-star analyst expects Expand Energy to generate FCF per share of about $10 in FY28, up from the prior estimate of about $8 at his mid-cycle price forecast of $3.50/MMBtu Henry Hub. Mehta raised his FCF estimate to reflect an improved outlook for share repurchases, operational efficiencies, and gas pricing realizations.

Furthermore, the analyst expects the recently announced $1.25 billion Twin Eagle acquisition to enhance the competitive positioning of the combined business to expand to premium markets and capture incremental deals in the power and LNG end markets.

Mehta ranks No. 449 among more than 12,490 analysts tracked by TipRanks. His ratings have been successful 64% of the time, delivering an average return of 12.1%. See Expand Energy Insider Trading on TipRanks.

Mehta is also bullish on Diamondback Energy, an independent oil and natural gas company focused on energy reserves that are primarily in the Permian Basin in West Texas. The company recently paid a base cash dividend of $1.10 per share for the second quarter of 2026. FANG stock offers a dividend yield of 2.2%.

Mehta increased his price target on FANG stock to $220 from $212 and reiterated a buy rating, citing the company's capital-efficient volume growth as oil prices remain high amid persistent supply disruption in the Middle East.

"We remain constructive on FANG, a high-quality, pure-play Permian Basin operator that continues to drive incremental capital efficiencies and strong well productivity relative to peers," said Mehta.

Also, the analyst said that the removal of a minimum return of capital commitment gives Diamondback more flexibility in taking capital allocation decisions amid high oil price volatility and macro uncertainty.

Mehta added that Diamondback sees a favorable environment for production growth, driven by the potential need for global inventory restocking. He highlighted that during Q2 2026, FANG's production volumes of 1,018 Mboe/d exceeded the high end of the company's guidance, driven by a stronger-than-expected natural gas output from Barnett development and improved downstream gas marketing.

Overall, Mehta is optimistic about Diamondback's growth and sees more upside in the stock, given higher production estimates, solid productivity and a deepening position in the Barnett shale formation. See Diamondback Energy Financials on TipRanks.
